title: Linear Regression 1: Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Key Assumptions of Linear Regression
Linear regression relies on several assumptions. Understanding these assumptions helps ensure valid statistical inference and reliable predictions.

1. Linearity

The relationship between predictor(s) and outcome is linear.
If the true relationship is curved but we fit a straight line, predictions will be systematically biased.
We can visually check by drawing a scatterplot.
If violated, consider transforming variables (log, square root) or using polynomial terms.



2. Independence of Observations

Each observation’s residual is unrelated to others’ residuals.
Correlated errors (e.g., repeated measures, clustered data) underestimate standard errors, making p-values too small.
Know your data structure and study design (longitudinal? clustered?)
If violated, use mixed models, clustered standard errors, or time-series methods.



3. Homoscedasticity (Equal Variance)

Variance of residuals is constant across all fitted values.
Unequal variance (heteroscedasticity) makes standard errors unreliable and confidence intervals inaccurate.
We can visually inspect by drawing a Residuals vs Fitted plot (vertical spread should be roughly equal across x-axis)
If violated, use robust standard errors or transform Y.



4. Normality of Residuals

Residuals follow a normal distribution.
Critical for valid p-values and confidence intervals
We can visually inspect using a Q-Q plot (points should follow the diagonal line)
If violated, consider transforming Y or using robust methods.



5. No (Perfect) Multicollinearity (Multiple Regression Only)

Predictors are not highly correlated with each other.
High correlation between predictors inflates standard errors, making coefficients unstable and hard to interpret.
We can check the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF; VIF > 10 indicates problematic multicollinearity)
If violated, remove redundant predictors, combine correlated predictors, or use penalized regression (we will cover this later in the semester).




Summary: Which Plot Checks Which Assumption?



Assumption
Primary Diagnostic




Linearity
Residuals vs Fitted (look for no pattern)


Independence
Know your study design


Homoscedasticity
Residuals vs Fitted (equal vertical spread)


Normality
Q-Q plot


Multicollinearity
VIF values (not a plot)

title: Linear Regression 1: Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Diagnostic Plots
We can draw diagnostic plots by using the plot() function in R.

which = 1: Residuals vs Fitted
which = 2: Q-Q plot


# Create diagnostic plots
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))  # 1 row, 2 columns
plot(model_multiple, which = 1) # Residual vs. fitted plot
plot(model_multiple, which = 2) # Q-Q plot
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))  # Reset to default







Figure 6: Regression diagnostic plots






Interpreting the Two Standard Diagnostic Plots
Plot 1: Residuals vs Fitted (left)

What to look for: Random scatter around horizontal line at 0
What it checks: Linearity and homoscedasticity
Good sign: No pattern, equal spread across x-axis
Red flags:

Curved pattern = non-linearity
Funnel shape = heteroscedasticity


Plot 2: Normal Q-Q (Quantile-Quantile; right)

A Q-Q plot compares the distribution of your residuals to a theoretical normal distribution.
What to look for: Points following the diagonal reference line
What it checks: Normality of residuals
Points close around the diagonal indicate residuals are normally distributed

title: Linear Regression 1: Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Checking for Multicollinearity
Multicollinearity occurs when predictors are highly correlated, which can:

Inflate standard errors
Make individual coefficients unstable
Lead to counterintuitive results


Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)
VIF quantifies how much multicollinearity inflates the variance of regression coefficients.
How VIF works:
For each predictor \(X_j\):

Regress \(X_j\) on all other predictors
Get \(R^2_j\) from that regression (how well other predictors explain \(X_j\))
Calculate: \(\text{VIF}_j = \frac{1}{1 - R^2_j}\)


Rule of Thumb: VIF > 10 (or Tolerance < 0.1) indicates problematic multicollinearity.

We can get VIF values by using the vif() function in R (to use it, we first need to load the package car).

# Calculate VIF
vif_values <- car::vif(model_multiple)
vif_values

              age    severity_score num_comorbidities 
         1.001982          1.003890          1.002301 


As all of them are less than 10, they are not highly correlated with each other.

title: Linear Regression 1: Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Key Takeaways

Simple vs. Multiple Linear Regression

Simple regression: Examines how one factor relates to an outcome (“If X increases by 1, how much does Y change?”)
Multiple regression: Examines how several factors together relate to an outcome, showing each factor’s unique contribution while holding others constant



How OLS Finds the Best Line

Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) finds the line that minimizes the sum of squared residuals
“Residuals” = vertical distance between actual data points and the fitted line



Model Fit: R²

R² tells you what percentage of variation your model explains
Adjusted R² is better for multiple regression (accounts for number of predictors)
Higher is better, but context matters



Making Predictions

Use fitted models to predict outcomes for new situations
Useful for “what-if” scenarios and planning



Interpreting Coefficients
Ask three questions for each coefficient:

Direction: Positive or negative relationship?
Magnitude: How large is the effect practically?
Significance: Is p < 0.05? (But practical significance matters too!)

In multiple regression, coefficients show effects while controlling for other variables.


Multicollinearity

When predictors are highly correlated, coefficients become unstable and can even flip signs
Check: VIF > 10 indicates problems
Solution: Remove or combine correlated predictors

title: Decision Trees for Healthcare Prediction
text:
Imagine you’re the CFO of a large hospital system. Every year, you need to budget for patient care costs. Some patients cost $2,000 annually, others cost $200,000. Your board wants accurate predictions so you can:

Set appropriate insurance premiums
Allocate resources to high-risk patients
Plan staffing and capacity

You have data on thousands of patients (e.g., their age, medical conditions, past emergency room visits, insurance type, etc). In prior lectures, we learned how to use (penalized) regression models. But here’s the problem: healthcare costs don’t work in simple, linear, additive ways.
Consider two patients:

Patient A: 25 years old with diabetes → might cost $3,000/year
Patient B: 75 years old with diabetes → might cost $30,000/year

The effect of diabetes is completely different depending on age! With regular regression, you’d have to manually tell the computer “create an age × diabetes interaction term.” But what if there are dozens of such interactions? You’d never find them all.
This is where decision trees shine: they automatically discover these complex patterns.









Note📘 Terminology: Decision Trees vs. Regression Trees



“Decision Tree” is the umbrella term for tree-based models. There are two main types:

Classification Trees: Predict categories (e.g., “Will this patient be readmitted?” → Yes/No)
Regression Trees: Predict continuous numbers (e.g., “What will this patient cost?” → $15,247)

In this lecture, we’ll cover regression trees because we’re predicting annual healthcare costs (a continuous dollar amount). However, the core concepts and methods apply to both types, so we’ll use “decision tree” as the general term throughout. Just remember: when we say “decision tree,” we specifically mean the regression tree variety!


Think of a decision tree like a game of “20 Questions” for predicting patient costs:





graph TD
    A["Patient over 65?<br/>All Patients"] --> |YES| B["Hospitalized in<br/>past year?"]
    A --> |NO| C["Any chronic<br/>conditions?"]

    B --> |YES| D["Heart disease?"]
    B --> |NO| E["Predict: $15,000"]

    D --> |YES| F["Predict: $45,000"]
    D --> |NO| G["Predict: $25,000"]

    C --> |YES| H["Predict: $8,000"]
    C --> |NO| I["Predict: $2,500"]

    style G fill:#e8f4f8,stroke:#2c5aa0,stroke-width:3px
    style E fill:#e8f4f8,stroke:#2c5aa0,stroke-width:3px
    style H fill:#e8f4f8,stroke:#2c5aa0,stroke-width:3px
    style I fill:#e8f4f8,stroke:#2c5aa0,stroke-width:3px






How to read this diagram:

Start at the top box (“Patient over 65?”)
Follow the arrows based on YES vs. NO answers
End at a blue prediction box (called a “leaf”)
Each question splits patients into smaller, more similar groups

Each final prediction is based on the average cost of similar patients in your historical data.



Decision trees are particularly powerful for healthcare analytics because:


Doctors already use tree-like decision rules: “If patient has chest pain AND is over 50 AND has diabetes → run cardiac workup.” Trees formalize this intuitive reasoning.




Interactions: Automatically discover whether a factor matters more depending on other factors (e.g., heart disease matters more for elderly patients)
Non-linear relationships: Don’t assume age has a constant effect across all ranges
Mixed data types: Handle both numbers (age, lab values) and categories (gender, insurance type)




You can literally draw the tree and show it to decision makers. For example: “This patient is over 65, has been to the ER 3 times, and has heart disease, so we predict they will be high-cost.”




No need to standardize variables
Can handle missing data
No assumptions about data distributions





By the end of this session, you will be able to:

Explain what decision trees are to others using simple, non-technical language
Read and interpret tree diagrams to understand why specific predictions are made
Understand why trees can “overfit” and how to prevent it (finding the right tree size)
Build decision trees in R to predict healthcare outcomes (costs, length of stay, etc.)
Evaluate whether your tree is making good predictions using test data

title: Decision Trees for Healthcare Prediction
section: 2.1 The Basic Idea: Divide and Conquer
text:
2.1 The Basic Idea: Divide and Conquer
Let’s build intuition with a simple example. Imagine you have 100 patients and you want to predict their annual healthcare costs. Here’s what a decision tree does:
Step 1: Start with everyone in one group

All 100 patients together
Average cost: $15,000
But there’s huge variation: some cost $1,000, others $100,000
We can measure how much error we have in predictions when only the average cost is used

Step 2: Find the best split
The algorithm looks at every variable and asks: “What single split would best separate high-cost from low-cost patients?”
Maybe it finds:

Patients with prior hospitalizations (n=20) → average $45,000
Patients without prior hospitalizations (n=80) → average $8,000

If these predictions are more accurate than predicting $15,000 for everyone, we use this split.
Step 3: Repeat for each group
Now take those 80 patients without prior hospitalizations. Can we do better than predicting $8,000 for all of them?
Maybe split by age:

Under 50 (n=50) → average $4,000
Over 50 (n=30) → average $14,000

Step 4: Keep going until groups are homogeneous
Continue this process until each final group (called a “leaf”) contains patients with similar healthcare costs.

title: Decision Trees for Healthcare Prediction
section: 2.2 How Does the Tree Decide Where to Split?
text:
2.2 How Does the Tree Decide Where to Split?
Simple Answer: It tries every possible split and picks the one that reduces prediction errors the most.

2.2.1 Example: Splitting on Age
Let’s say we’re considering: “Should we split at age 50?”
Before split: 100 patients, average cost = $15,000

Some patients cost $50,000, some cost $2,000
Our predictions are pretty bad!

After splitting at age 50:

Group 1 (Age < 50): 60 patients, average = $7,000

Most patients are close to $7,000
Prediction errors are smaller

Group 2 (Age ≥ 50): 40 patients, average = $26,000

Most patients are close to $26,000
Prediction errors are smaller


The algorithm measures whether our prediction errors get smaller. If yes, it’s a good split!
The algorithm tries EVERY possible split (age 30, age 31, age 32, etc., and also diabetes yes/no, prior ER visits 0 vs. 1+, etc.) and picks the winner.

title: Decision Trees for Healthcare Prediction
text:
2.3 Why “Recursive”?
Recursive means the algorithm repeats the same process over and over:

Look at a group of patients
Find the best way to split them into two groups
For each new group, go back to step 1
Stop when groups are small or homogeneous enough

Think of it like organizing a filing cabinet:

First drawer: “Active” vs. “Inactive” patients
Within “Active”: “High-risk” vs. “Low-risk”
Within “High-risk”: “Diabetes” vs. “No diabetes”
And so on…

Each level of the tree makes the groups more specific and similar.

title: Decision Trees for Healthcare Prediction
section: 2.4 Optimal Tree Size: Not Too Big, Not Too Small
text:
2.4 Optimal Tree Size: Not Too Big, Not Too Small

2.4.1 The Danger of Trees That Are Too Big (Overfitting)
Imagine a tree that keeps splitting until each final group has only 1-2 patients:
Patient A, age 67, diabetic, 2 ER visits → Predicted cost: $43,127

This is patient A’s actual cost from last year!
But is this a good prediction for similar (new) patients?
No! Patient A might have had an unusual surgery that year or other conditions

This is overfitting: The tree has memorized the specific patients in your data, including all the random variation (lucky vs. unlucky years, unusual events, etc.). When we apply the same rules to new patients, this may not perform well.


2.4.2 The Danger of Trees That Are Too Small (Underfitting)
On the other hand, a tree with only 1-2 splits might be too simple:
All patients → Predicted cost: $15,000

This is useless! We know costs vary wildly
We’re ignoring useful information

This is underfitting: The tree is too simple to capture real patterns.


2.4.3 The Solution: Finding the “Just Right” or Optimal Tree Size
We need to find the sweet spot. Here’s how:
Step 1: Grow a large tree

Let it split many times
Don’t worry about overfitting yet

Step 2: Test different tree sizes

Prune back to different sizes (15 leaves, 10 leaves, 5 leaves, 3 leaves…)
For each size, measure prediction accuracy on separate test data

Step 3: Pick the size that performs best on test data

Not on training data (that would just give us the biggest tree)
On fresh data the tree hasn’t seen

Think of it like teaching someone to cook.

Too few instructions (“cook the chicken”) = underfit.
Too many instructions (“heat to exactly 347.2°F for 37 minutes and 12 seconds”) = overfit.
The right amount: “cook until internal temperature reaches 165°F and juices run clear” = just right!



2.4.4 Cross-Validation: The Smart Way to Find the Right Size
The Problem: Why We Can’t Use Test Data for Model Selection
You might think: “I’ll just try different tree sizes and pick the one that performs best on my test set!” But this creates a subtle problem:
Bad Approach:

Try 5-leaf tree → test on test set → error = $8,000
Try 10-leaf tree → test on test set → error = $7,500
Try 15-leaf tree → test on test set → error = $7,200 ✓ Best!
Pick 15-leaf tree and report: “Our model has $7,200 error”

You’ve now peeked at the test set multiple times and chose the model specifically because it performed well on this data. Your reported error ($7,200) is overly optimistic. It won’t reflect true performance on future patients you haven’t seen yet!
The Solution: Cross-Validation on Training Data Only
Keep your test set locked away until the very end! Instead:

Split once: 70% training, 30% test (lock the test set away!)
Within training data, split into 10 pieces for cross-validation (the number of folds can vary)
For each tree size:

Train on 9 pieces, validate on the 10th
Repeat 10 times (each piece gets to be validation set)
Average the validation errors across all 10 folds

Pick tree size with best average cross-validation error
Build final model on ALL training data
Finally, evaluate once on test set for honest performance

This way, the test set truly represents “future patients” (non-trained data) you haven’t peeked at!

title: Decision Trees for Healthcare Prediction
section: 2.5 When Should You Use Decision Trees?
text:
2.5 When Should You Use Decision Trees?
Decision Trees Are GREAT For:
1. Explaining to Non-Technical Audiences

“Here’s exactly why we predict this patient is high-risk”
Can draw the tree easily (like in PowerPoint)
Creates clear, actionable patient segments

2. Complex, Interactive Relationships

When effects depend on context (diabetes matters more for elderly patients)
When you don’t know which interactions matter in advance
When relationships are non-linear (age 70→75 might matter more than 30→35)

3. Mixed Data Types

Combining numbers (age, lab values) and categories (gender, insurance)
No need to create dummy variables manually

4. Quick Prototyping

Fast to build and interpret
Good for initial exploration

Decision Trees Are LESS GREAT For:
1. When Relationships Are Smooth, Linear, and Additive

If cost really does just go up $250 per year of age for everyone (constant effect), linear regression would be simpler and more accurate

2. Small Datasets

Trees need enough data to split multiple times. In general, trees with <100 observations might not split well

3. When You Need Smooth Predictions

Trees create “step functions” where everyone in a group gets the same prediction. When smooth, continuous predictions are needed, tree models may not be ideal.

4. Extrapolation

Trees can’t predict beyond the range of your data. For example, if oldest patient in the data is 85, can’t reliably predict for 95-year-old.

title: Decision Trees for Healthcare Prediction
text:
3.1 Step 1: Loading Our Tools
Think of this like getting your tools ready before starting a project. We need special R packages, rpart (Recursive Partitioning And Regression Trees) for building and visualizing trees.

title: Decision Trees for Healthcare Prediction
text:
3.2 Step 2: Creating Our Patient Dataset
The Context: You’re analyzing a health system with 1,000 patients. You want to predict their annual healthcare costs based on things like age, medical conditions, and past utilization.
We’ll create simulated data that mimics real-world healthcare:

Complex relationships: Diabetes costs more for elderly patients than young ones (interaction!)
Realistic cost distribution: Most patients are low-cost, some are very expensive
Multiple types of information: Numbers (age), categories (insurance type), yes/no (diabetes)

Don’t worry about understanding every line of code here—focus on what we’re creating:

# Step 2a: Create 1,000 patients with various characteristics
n <- 1000  # Our sample size

healthcare_data <- data.frame(
  # Basic demographics
  age = round(runif(n, 18, 85)),  # Age between 18-85
  sex = sample(c("Male", "Female"), n, replace = TRUE),

  # Health indicators
  bmi = round(rnorm(n, 28, 6), 1),  # Body Mass Index
  smoker = sample(c(0, 1), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.8, 0.2)),  # 20% smokers

  # Medical conditions (we'll fill these in next based on age)
  diabetes = NA,
  hypertension = NA,
  heart_disease = NA,

  # Insurance coverage
  insurance = sample(c("Private", "Medicare", "Medicaid", "Uninsured"),
                     n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.5, 0.25, 0.15, 0.1)),

  # Past healthcare use (higher numbers = more past utilization)
  prior_er_visits = rpois(n, lambda = 0.5),
  prior_hospitalizations = rpois(n, lambda = 0.15),

  # Geographic region
  region = sample(c("Northeast", "Midwest", "South", "West"), n, replace = TRUE)
)

# Step 2b: Generate medical conditions (more likely for older patients)
# This makes our data realistic - older people tend to have more conditions
healthcare_data <- healthcare_data %>%
  mutate(
    # Diabetes: more common with age and higher BMI
    diabetes = rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-3 + 0.03 * age + 0.05 * bmi)),

    # High blood pressure: more common with age
    hypertension = rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-2 + 0.04 * age)),

    # Heart disease: more common with age, smoking, and other conditions
    heart_disease = rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-4 + 0.05 * age + 0.5 * smoker +
                                         0.3 * diabetes + 0.3 * hypertension)),

    # Total number of chronic conditions per patient
    n_conditions = diabetes + hypertension + heart_disease
  )

# Step 2c: Generate annual healthcare costs
# We're building in complex patterns that our decision tree will discover:
# - Non-linear age effects (costs accelerate with age)
# - Interactions (conditions cost more for elderly patients)
# - Variation (some randomness, like in real life)

healthcare_data <- healthcare_data %>%
  mutate(
    # Base cost increases with age (and accelerates - that's the age^2 part)
    base_cost = 1000 + 50 * age + 0.5 * age^2,

    # Costs from chronic conditions
    # IMPORTANT: Notice we multiply age × n_conditions - this is an INTERACTION
    # Conditions cost more for older patients!
    condition_cost = 3000 * diabetes + 2500 * hypertension +
                     5000 * heart_disease +
                     50 * age * n_conditions,  # <-- The interaction

    # Costs from past healthcare use
    utilization_cost = 2000 * prior_er_visits + 15000 * prior_hospitalizations,

    # Costs from behaviors
    behavior_cost = 1500 * smoker + 50 * pmax(bmi - 30, 0),

    # Insurance affects recorded costs
    insurance_effect = case_when(
      insurance == "Private" ~ 1.0,
      insurance == "Medicare" ~ 1.1,  # Medicare patients use more services
      insurance == "Medicaid" ~ 0.9,
      insurance == "Uninsured" ~ 0.6  # Uninsured use less (unfortunately)
    ),

    # Combine everything to get final cost
    expected_cost = (base_cost + condition_cost + utilization_cost +
                     behavior_cost) * insurance_effect,

    # Add some randomness (real life isn't perfectly predictable!)
    annual_cost = round(expected_cost * exp(rnorm(n, 0, 0.3)))
  ) %>%
  # Remove intermediate calculation columns (we just need annual_cost)
  select(-base_cost, -condition_cost, -utilization_cost,
         -behavior_cost, -insurance_effect, -expected_cost)

# Step 2d: Convert text variables to proper format for R
# R needs categorical variables (like "Male"/"Female") as "factors"
healthcare_data <- healthcare_data %>%
  mutate(
    sex = factor(sex),
    insurance = factor(insurance),
    region = factor(region),
    smoker = factor(smoker, labels = c("No", "Yes")),
    diabetes = factor(diabetes, labels = c("No", "Yes")),
    hypertension = factor(hypertension, labels = c("No", "Yes")),
    heart_disease = factor(heart_disease, labels = c("No", "Yes"))
  )

# Show what we created
head(healthcare_data)

What we just created:

1,000 patients with realistic characteristics
13 variables total:

11 predictor variables: age, sex, BMI, smoking, 3 chronic conditions (diabetes, hypertension, heart disease), insurance, prior ER visits, prior hospitalizations, region
1 derived variable: n_conditions (total count of chronic conditions; we will not use this one)
1 outcome variable: annual_cost (what we want to predict)

Hidden complexity: The relationship between these variables and cost includes non-linear effects and interactions - perfect for testing decision trees!


3.2.1 Step 3: Understanding Our Data
Before building a decision tree, let’s look at what we’re working with. This helps us know what patterns to expect.

# Summary statistics for the outcome
# (We'll display these as markdown text below the chart)

# Distribution plots
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

# Cost distribution
hist(healthcare_data$annual_cost / 1000, breaks = 30,
     main = "Distribution of Annual Healthcare Costs",
     xlab = "Annual Cost ($1000s)", col = "steelblue", border = "white")

# Costs by age
plot(healthcare_data$age, healthcare_data$annual_cost / 1000,
     main = "Costs vs. Age",
     xlab = "Age (years)", ylab = "Annual Cost ($1000s)",
     col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.5), pch = 16)
lines(lowess(healthcare_data$age, healthcare_data$annual_cost / 1000),
      col = "red", lwd = 2)

# Costs by number of conditions
boxplot(annual_cost / 1000 ~ n_conditions, data = healthcare_data,
        main = "Costs by Number of Chronic Conditions",
        xlab = "Number of Conditions", ylab = "Annual Cost ($1000s)",
        col = "steelblue")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))








Note: While we won’t include n_conditions in our tree model (since it’s redundant with the individual condition variables), it’s still useful for understanding cost patterns in our exploratory analysis.
Key Statistics About Our Data:

Average (mean) cost: Around $17,000 per patient per year
Middle (median) cost: Lower than the mean (about $15,000)
Range: From a few hundred dollars to over $100,000
Distribution: Right-skewed (most patients low-cost, some very high-cost)

What the charts tell us:

Most patients are low-cost, some are very high-cost - this is typical in healthcare
Costs increase with age - especially after age 60
More chronic conditions = higher costs - but the relationship isn’t simple
Lots of variation - two patients with similar characteristics might have different costs

Now let’s build a decision tree to predict these costs!

title: Decision Trees for Healthcare Prediction
section: 3.3 Step 4: Building Your First Decision Tree
text:
3.3 Step 4: Building Your First Decision Tree
This is the exciting part! We’re going to build a decision tree that automatically discovers patterns in our data.

3.3.1 The Basic Command
Building a tree in R is surprisingly simple. We can use the rpart function in R. It’s similar to the lm() function you learned for regression:

# Build the decision tree!
# This is the main command - notice it looks like lm()
cost_tree <- rpart(
  # Formula: predict annual_cost using all these variables
  formula = annual_cost ~ age + sex + bmi + smoker + diabetes +
            hypertension + heart_disease + insurance +
            prior_er_visits + prior_hospitalizations + region,

  # Which data to use
  data = healthcare_data,

  # method = "anova" means we're predicting a number (not a category)
  method = "anova"

  # Note: Cross-validation happens automatically!
  # rpart performs 10-fold CV by default (controlled by xval = 10 parameter)
  # The CV results are stored in cost_tree$cptable (we'll see this later)
)

# Look at the text summary (not very readable, we'll visualize it next!)
print(cost_tree)

The text output is hard to read, so let’s visualize it!


3.3.2 Visualizing the Tree
Trees are meant to be seen, not read as text. Let’s create a visual diagram using the rpart.plot function:

# Create a beautiful tree diagram!
rpart.plot(
  cost_tree,
  type = 4,                 # Show all the information
  extra = 101,              # Show number and percentage of patients in each group
  under = TRUE,             # Put numbers under the boxes (easier to read)
  fallen.leaves = TRUE,     # Line up the bottom boxes
  branch = 0.3,             # How curved the branches are
  box.palette = "Blues",    # Color scheme (blue boxes)
  shadow.col = "gray",      # Add subtle shadows
  main = "Decision Tree for Healthcare Cost Prediction",
  cex = 0.8,                # Text size
  roundint = TRUE,          # Round to integers (no decimals for dollar amounts)
  digits = 5                # Use up to 5 digits (prevents scientific notation)
)










3.3.3 How to Read This Tree Diagram
Think of it like a flowchart for patient triage:

Start at the top box (the “root”)

Contains ALL patients
Shows average cost for everyone

Follow the labeled arrows

Each split asks a yes/no question
Follow the arrow labeled YES or NO based on the patient’s characteristics
The arrows show you which path to take

End at a bottom box (a “leaf”)

This is your prediction!
Shows the average cost for patients in that group

The deeper you go, the more specific the groups

First split: broad groups (e.g., old vs. young)
Later splits: narrow groups (e.g., elderly diabetics who’ve been hospitalized)




3.3.4 Let’s Trace a Patient Through the Tree
Imagine a new patient walks in. Here’s how to predict their cost:

# Create an example patient
example_patient <- data.frame(
  age = 72,

text:
3.4 Controlling Tree Complexity

3.4.1 Understanding the Control Parameters
The rpart() function has several parameters that control how the tree grows. Understanding these is crucial for building effective models:

# Display default control parameters
defaults <- rpart.control()

Default rpart Control Parameters:
The rpart function has several “knobs” you can turn to control tree growth:
1. minsplit (default = 20)

Minimum observations required to attempt a split (i.e., “Don’t split groups smaller than 20 patients”)
Lower values → more splits → larger trees

2. minbucket (default = 7)

Minimum observations in any terminal node (leaf; i.e., “Each final group must have at least 7 patients”)
Lower values → smaller final groups → more overfitting risk

3. cp (complexity parameter, default = 0.01)

Controls pruning - this is the most important parameter!
Lower values → less pruning → larger trees
We’ll use cross-validation to find the optimal cp

4. maxdepth (default = 30)

Maximum depth of tree (number of levels)
Higher values → deeper trees → more interactions captured
Usually not a limiting factor



3.4.2 The Complexity Parameter (cp)
The complexity parameter cp is the most important tuning parameter. It controls pruning - how the tree decides whether a split is worth keeping:

A split is only kept if it reduces prediction errors by a meaningful amount (controlled by cp)
Higher cp → fewer splits → simpler trees
Lower cp → more splits → complex trees

Let’s see how cp affects tree size:

# Fit trees with different cp values
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

cp_values <- c(0.1, 0.03, 0.01, 0.001)

for (cp_val in cp_values) {
  tree_temp <- rpart(
    annual_cost ~ age + sex + bmi + smoker + diabetes +
                  hypertension + heart_disease + insurance +
                  prior_er_visits + prior_hospitalizations + region,
    data = healthcare_data,
    method = "anova",
    control = rpart.control(cp = cp_val)
  )

  # Count terminal nodes
  n_leaves <- sum(tree_temp$frame$var == "<leaf>")

  rpart.plot(tree_temp,
             main = paste0("cp = ", cp_val, " (", n_leaves, " leaves)"),
             cex = 0.6,
             roundint = TRUE,
             digits = 5)
}







par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

As cp decreases, the tree grows larger with more terminal nodes. The challenge is finding the right balance—enough complexity to capture true patterns but not so much that we overfit.


3.4.3 Cross-Validation for Optimal Pruning






Tip🔍 Where Does Cross-Validation Happen?



Answer: Automatically inside rpart()!
When you call rpart(), it performs 10-fold cross-validation behind the scenes and stores the results in the tree’s $cptable component. You don’t need to explicitly code the CV - it happens automatically!
If you want to control it: - xval = 10 (default): 10-fold cross-validation - xval = 5: 5-fold cross-validation - xval = 0: Turn off CV (not recommended!)


Now let’s access those cross-validation results that rpart() computed for us:

# Fit a full tree (small cp to grow large)
# Note: This automatically performs 10-fold CV!
full_tree <- rpart(
  annual_cost ~ age + sex + bmi + smoker + diabetes +
                hypertension + heart_disease + insurance +
                prior_er_visits + prior_hospitalizations + region,
  data = healthcare_data,
  method = "anova",
  control = rpart.control(cp = 0.001)  # Grow a large tree
)

# Display the cross-validation results (stored in $cptable)
print(full_tree$cptable)

Understanding the Cross-Validation Table (cptable):
Each row shows results for a different tree size:

CP: Complexity parameter value
nsplit: Number of splits in the tree
rel error: Training error (relative to simplest tree)
xerror: Cross-validated error (what we care about!)
xstd: Standard error of the CV error

What to look for: The tree size (nsplit) that has the lowest xerror!


3.4.4 Visualizing Cross-Validation Results
Let’s plot the cross-validation errors to find the optimal tree size:

# Plot cross-validation results
plotcp(full_tree)







# Find the cp with lowest cross-validation error
cp_table <- full_tree$cptable
optimal_cp <- cp_table[which.min(cp_table[, "xerror"]), "CP"]

How to Read This Plot:

X-axis (top): Size of tree (number of terminal nodes)
X-axis (bottom): Corresponding cp values
Y-axis: Cross-validation error (relative scale)
Dotted horizontal line: Minimum CV error + 1 standard error (1-SE rule threshold)
Goal: Find the lowest point on the curve (minimum xerror)

What we’re doing: We pick the cp that corresponds to the lowest point on this curve. That’s our optimal tree complexity!
Note: The dotted line shows the 1-SE rule threshold (a more conservative approach), but we’re using the simpler method of just picking the minimum point, which is 0.0024461.


3.4.5 Pruning the Tree
Now let’s prune our tree to the optimal size (remove less meaningful branches):

# Prune to optimal cp
pruned_tree <- prune(full_tree, cp = optimal_cp)

# Visualize the pruned tree
rpart.plot(
  pruned_tree,
  type = 4,
  extra = 101,
  under = TRUE,
  fallen.leaves = TRUE,
  box.palette = "Blues",
  main = paste0("Pruned Tree (cp = ", round(optimal_cp, 4), ")"),
  cex = 0.8,
  roundint = TRUE,
  digits = 5
)







# Compare tree sizes
n_leaves_full <- sum(full_tree$frame$var == "<leaf>")
n_leaves_pruned <- sum(pruned_tree$frame$var == "<leaf>")

Tree Size Comparison:

Full (unpruned) tree: 47 leaf nodes
Pruned tree: 27 leaf nodes

By pruning, we’ve created a simpler tree that’s easier to interpret while maintaining good predictive performance!

title: Decision Trees for Healthcare Prediction
text:
3.5 Evaluating Model Performance

3.5.1 Train-Test Split Approach
For a fair evaluation, we should test our model on data it hasn’t seen during training. Let’s split our data and evaluate performance properly. Same as others, let’s use a 70:30 split.

# Create train-test split (70-30)
train_idx <- sample(1:nrow(healthcare_data), 0.7 * nrow(healthcare_data))
train_data <- healthcare_data[train_idx, ]
test_data <- healthcare_data[-train_idx, ]

Data Split:

Training set: 700 patients (70%) - used to build the tree
Test set: 300 patients (30%) - held out to evaluate performance

This split ensures we evaluate the model on patients it has never seen before!


3.5.2 Building and Evaluating the Tree
Let’s build a tree model using the training dataset.

# Fit tree on training data
tree_train <- rpart(
  annual_cost ~ age + sex + bmi + smoker + diabetes +
                hypertension + heart_disease + insurance +
                prior_er_visits + prior_hospitalizations + region,
  data = train_data,
  method = "anova",
  control = rpart.control(cp = 0.001)
)

# Find optimal cp (lowest cross-validation error)
best_cp <- tree_train$cptable[which.min(tree_train$cptable[,"xerror"]), "CP"]

# Prune the tree to optimal size
tree_final <- prune(tree_train, cp = best_cp)

# Make predictions on test set
predictions <- predict(tree_final, test_data)

# Calculate performance metrics
actual <- test_data$annual_cost

# Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) - our primary metric
rmse <- sqrt(mean((actual - predictions)^2))

# R-squared - how much variation we explain
ss_res <- sum((actual - predictions)^2)
ss_tot <- sum((actual - mean(actual))^2)
r_squared <- 1 - (ss_res / ss_tot)

Test Set Performance:
How well does our tree predict costs for new patients? We’ll focus on two key metrics:
1. RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error): $8,498

This is the most common metric for comparing prediction models
Interpretation: “On average, our predictions are off by about $8,498”
Lower is better!

2. R-squared: 0.601

You’ve seen this before in regression!
Interpretation: “Our model explains 60.06% of the variation in healthcare costs”
Higher is better (ranges from 0 to 1)



3.5.3 Visualizing Predictions vs. Actual
Let’s see how well our predictions match actual costs:

# Create prediction comparison plot
pred_df <- data.frame(
  Actual = actual,
  Predicted = predictions
)

ggplot(pred_df, aes(x = Actual/1000, y = Predicted/1000)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Regression Tree: Predicted vs. Actual Healthcare Costs",
    x = "Actual Cost ($1000s)",
    y = "Predicted Cost ($1000s)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  coord_fixed()








Points along the red dashed line represent perfect predictions. The closer the data points are to the red dashed line, the better the model performed.

title: Decision Trees for Healthcare Prediction
text:
4.1 What We Learned Today
1. Decision Trees Are a Different Way to Think About Prediction

Instead of equations, we create groups of similar patients
Each group gets a prediction based on historical averages
Works like a game of “20 questions” to classify patients

2. Trees Automatically Find Complex Patterns

They discover interactions (diabetes costs more for elderly patients)
They handle non-linear relationships (age effects that accelerate)
No need to manually specify these patterns!

3. Trees Are Easy to Explain

Visual diagrams anyone can understand
Clear decision rules for each prediction
Great for presenting to non-technical stakeholders

4. But Trees Need Careful Tuning

Too big → overfitting (memorizing noise)
Too small → underfitting (missing patterns)
Use cross-validation to find an optimal size

5. Trees vs. Regression: Different Tools for Different Jobs

Trees: Complex interactions, automatic feature discovery, easy to explain
Regression: Smooth relationships, smaller datasets, interpretable coefficients
Try both and compare!

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
t-tests are among the most fundamental and widely-used statistical tools that allow us to make data-driven decisions by comparing means and determining whether observed differences are simply due to chance or not.
Consider this scenario:

A hospital administrator notices that their emergency department’s average waiting time appears to be 52 minutes, while the regional standard is 45 minutes. Is this 7-minute difference a systematic problem that needs addressing, or could it simply be random variation in the data? This is exactly the type of question that t-tests help us answer.

t-tests are to compare means. Specifically, they determine whether observed mean differences are statistically significant—that is, whether the differences we see in our sample data likely reflect true differences in the population, or whether they could have occurred simply by chance. This distinction is critical because acting on random noise can waste resources, while ignoring real problems can harm outcomes.



There are three types of t-tests, each designed for different research scenarios:








Test Type
Purpose
Example




One-sample
Compare a sample mean to a known or hypothesized value
Testing if average wait time differs from a 45-minute standard


Independent-samples
Compare means from two separate, unrelated groups
Comparing processing times between two different intake systems


Paired-samples
Compare two related measurements on the same subjects
Measuring scores before and after an intervention




The following sections will explain each test in detail, with worked examples and R code that you can apply to your own data.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
What is it?
A one-sample t-test is a statistical procedure that compares a sample mean to a known or hypothesized population value. It answers a fundamental question:

Is our sample mean significantly different from a specific benchmark, or could the difference we observe be due to random chance?

This test is particularly useful when you have a single group of observations and want to compare their average to some external standard or target value. For example, if there is a law regarding a maximum acceptable waiting time, or if industry benchmarks establish expected performance levels, the one-sample t-test helps you determine whether your organization is meeting those standards.

Key Components

One group of observations (your sample data)
One comparison value (a benchmark, standard, target, or known or hypothesized mean)

The test works by calculating how far your sample mean deviates from the comparison value, relative to the variability in your data. If this deviation is large enough, we conclude that the difference is unlikely to have occurred by chance alone.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
When to Use It
The one-sample t-test is appropriate whenever you need to compare your data against a fixed reference point. Common scenarios include:

Comparing performance against national or industry benchmarks

e.g.,) average length of stay compared to national average

Testing if outcomes meet target levels set by management or regulators

e.g.,) patient satisfaction scores vs. a target of 8.0

Evaluating if measurements achieve recommended standards

e.g.,) medication dosages achieving target blood levels

Assessing if operational metrics meet regulatory requirements

e.g.,) waiting times vs. regulatory standards

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
section: One-Sample t-test Scenario: ED Waiting Times
text:
One-Sample t-test Scenario: ED Waiting Times

Imagine you are an administrator at a hospital where the regional average emergency department waiting time is 45 minutes. Recently, you’ve received complaints that patients are waiting too long. To investigate, you randomly sample 30 patients and record their waiting times.
Your sample shows an average waiting time of 52 minutes. But before concluding that there’s a problem (i.e., the hospital is underperforming), you need to ask:

Is this difference of 7 minutes statistically significant, or could it simply be due to the natural variation we’d expect when taking a random sample?

This is precisely what the one-sample t-test will help us determine.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
Hypotheses
For our ED waiting times scenario, we set up our hypotheses as:

Null Hypothesis (H₀): μ = 45 (The hospital’s mean waiting time equals the 45-minute regional standard)
Alternative Hypothesis (H₁): μ ≠ 45 (The hospital’s mean waiting time differs from the standard)

The t-test will help us decide whether to reject H₀ based on our sample data.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
The Formula
The t-statistic is calculated as:
\[t = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt{n}}\]
Where:

\(\bar{X}\): sample mean (e.g., 52 minutes in our scenario)
\(\mu_0\): hypothesized/known mean (e.g., 45-minute benchmark)
\(s\): sample standard deviation (measures the spread of your data)
\(n\): sample size (e.g., 30 patients in our scenario)


Understanding the Formula
The t-statistic essentially measures how many standard errors the sample mean is away from the hypothesized value. Let’s break this down:

The numerator (\(\bar{X} - \mu_0\)) represents the difference between what we observed and what we expected under the null hypothesis. A larger difference suggests our sample may come from a population with a different mean.
The denominator (\(s / \sqrt{n}\)) is the standard error of the mean, which tells us how much variability we’d expect in sample means due to random sampling. Dividing by this standardizes our difference, allowing us to assess whether it’s large relative to the expected sampling variation.

A t-statistic close to zero means our sample mean is close to the benchmark. A t-statistic far from zero (either positive or negative) means our sample mean differs substantially from the benchmark, relative to the variability in our data.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
Example Calculation
Let’s work through a concrete example using our demonstration dataset. We have waiting times from 30 randomly selected ED patients:

# Extract ED waiting times from our dataset
waiting_times <- hospital_ops$ed_wait_time
mu_0 <- 45  # benchmark (regional average)

# Calculate statistics
n <- length(waiting_times)
x_bar <- mean(waiting_times)
s <- sd(waiting_times)

# Calculate t-statistic manually
t_stat <- (x_bar - mu_0) / (s / sqrt(n))



Sample size: 30


Sample mean: 46.2 minutes


Sample SD: 2.61 


Standard error: 0.48


t-statistic: 2.52


The t-statistic tells us how many standard errors our sample mean (approximately 46 minutes) is away from the benchmark (45 minutes). A large absolute t-value suggests the difference is unlikely to be due to chance.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
Visualizing the Data
Before running a statistical test, it’s always good practice to visualize your data. A histogram helps us understand the distribution of ED waiting times:

ggplot(hospital_ops, aes(x = ed_wait_time)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "steelblue", color = "white", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mu_0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = x_bar, color = "darkgreen", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = mu_0 - 0.5, y = 7, label = "Benchmark\n(45 min)", 
           color = "red", hjust = 1, size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = x_bar + 0.5, y = 7, label = paste0("Sample Mean\n(", round(x_bar, 1), " min)"), 
           color = "darkgreen", hjust = 0, size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of ED Waiting Times",
       subtitle = "Comparing sample mean (green) to benchmark (red dashed)",
       x = "Waiting Time (minutes)", y = "Number of Patients") +
  theme_minimal()








The visualization shows that most waiting times cluster between 42-50 minutes, and our sample mean (green line) is clearly above the 45-minute benchmark (red dashed line).

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
Visualizing the Null Distribution
Visualizing what we would expect to see if the null hypothesis were true (i.e., if the true population mean really were 45 minutes) helps us understand hypothesis testing. This is called the null distribution.
The graph below shows the t-distribution under the null hypothesis. The gray shaded areas in the tails represent the rejection regions; if our calculated t-statistic falls in these regions, we reject the null hypothesis at the α = 0.05 significance level.









Notice that our calculated t-statistic (the red vertical line) falls into the right rejection region. This tells us visually that our sample mean is significantly different from the benchmark (i.e., such an extreme result would be very unlikely if the true mean were actually 45 minutes).

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
Conducting one-sample t-test in R
In practice, we use R’s built-in t.test() function rather than calculating everything manually. This function handles all the computations and provides a complete summary of results:

# Perform one-sample t-test
result <- t.test(hospital_ops$ed_wait_time, mu = 45)
parameters(result)

One Sample t-test

Parameter    |  Mean | mu | Difference |         95% CI | t(29) |     p
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
ed_wait_time | 46.20 | 45 |       1.20 | [45.23, 47.17] |  2.52 | 0.017

Alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 45



Interpreting the Output
Let’s break down what each part of the output means:

t-statistic (2.52): This measures how far our sample mean is from the hypothesized value in standard error units. Our value is quite large, indicating a substantial deviation.
df (degrees of freedom = 29): This equals n - 1 and determines the shape of the t-distribution used for calculating the p-value.
p-value (0.0174): This is the probability of observing a t-statistic as extreme as ours (or more extreme) if the null hypothesis were true. Our very small p-value indicates this would be extremely unlikely.
95% confidence interval [45.23, 47.17]: We are 95% confident that the true population mean lies within this range. Because 45 is not contained in this interval, we can reject the null hypothesis.
Sample mean (46.2): The average of our observed waiting times.



Conclusion
Since the p-value is much less than 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis. The evidence strongly suggests that the hospital’s average ED waiting time is significantly higher than the 45-minute regional standard. This finding warrants investigation into the causes of the longer wait times and potential interventions to address the issue.


✏️ Practice: One-Sample t-Test






NoteYour Turn! (5 minutes)



A clinic wants to test if their average patient satisfaction score differs from the national average of 8.0 (out of 10). Use the patient_outcomes dataset.
Step 1: Explore the data

satisfaction_scores <- patient_outcomes$___

# Calculate descriptive statistics

  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +

  labs(title = "Distribution of Patient Satisfaction Scores",
       x = "Satisfaction Score", y = "Count") +

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
What is it?
An independent-samples t-test (also called a two-sample t-test) compares means from two different, unrelated groups to determine if they are significantly different from each other. Unlike the one-sample t-test where we compare against a fixed benchmark, here we’re asking:

Are these two group means significantly different from each other, or could the observed difference be due to random variation?

This test is fundamental for comparing any two distinct groups, such as different treatment groups, different facilities, different time periods, or any other meaningful categorization. The key requirement is that the groups must be independent, meaning that the observations in one group have no relationship to the observations in the other group.

Key Requirements

Two independent groups: The observations in one group must be completely unrelated to those in the other group. (e.g., the behavior of patients at Hospital A does not influence the behavior of patients at Hospital B)
Continuous outcome variable: The variable you’re measuring (e.g., processing time, satisfaction score, length of stay) must be measured on a continuous scale.



Why “Independent”?
The term “independent” distinguishes this test from the paired-samples t-test, which we will talk about next. In an independent-samples design, each observation belongs to only one group, and there’s no natural pairing between observations across groups. If you measured the same patients before and after treatment, that would require a paired test instead.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
When to Use It
The independent-samples t-test is appropriate whenever you want to compare two separate groups. Common scenarios include:

Comparing treatments: Is a new drug more effective than the standard treatment?
Comparing facilities or departments: Does one hospital have shorter wait times than another?
Intervention studies: Did the intervention group have better outcomes than the control group?
Demographic comparisons: Do outcomes differ between urban and rural facilities?

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
section: Independent-Samples t-test Scenario: Comparing Patient Intake Systems
text:
Independent-Samples t-test Scenario: Comparing Patient Intake Systems
Imagine your health system is considering whether to invest in digital intake systems (the registration process when patients first arrive) across all facilities. Currently, Hospital A uses a digital tablet-based intake system, while Hospital B uses traditional paper forms. Before making a system-wide investment, leadership wants to know:

Does the digital system actually result in faster processing times?

You collect processing time data from 20 randomly selected patients at each hospital. The question is whether any difference you observe represents a significant difference in system efficiency, or whether it could simply be due to natural variation in processing times.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
Hypotheses
For our intake systems comparison:

Null Hypothesis (H₀): μ₁ = μ₂ (Mean processing time is the same for both systems)
Alternative Hypothesis (H₁): μ₁ ≠ μ₂ (Mean processing times differ between systems)

The t-test will help us decide whether the observed difference is statistically significant.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
The Formula
The t-statistic for an independent-samples t-test is calculated as:
\[t = \frac{\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2}{s_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}}\]
Where the pooled standard deviation is:
\[s_p = \sqrt{\frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2 + (n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}}\]

Understanding the Formula

Numerator (\(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\)): The difference between the two sample means, which is the effect we are trying to evaluate.
Denominator: The standard error of the difference between means. This combines the information about variability from both groups to estimate how much variation we would expect in the difference between sample means due to random sampling.
Pooled standard deviation (\(s_p\)): This is a weighted average of the two groups’ standard deviations. We “pool” them because we assume both groups have the same population variance (homogeneity of variance assumption). The pooling gives more weight to the larger sample.

The resulting t-statistic tells us how many standard errors the observed difference is from zero (i.e., no difference; the same mean in both groups). A large absolute t-value suggests the groups significantly differ.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
What is it?
A paired-samples t-test (also called a dependent t-test or matched-pairs t-test) compares two related measurements on the same subjects or matched pairs. Unlike the independent-samples t-test where we compare different groups of people, here we’re asking:

Is there a significant change within the same individuals between two time points, conditions, or measures?

This test is particularly powerful because by measuring the same subjects twice, we can control for individual differences. Each person serves as their own control, which reduces variability and increases our ability to detect true effects.

Key Characteristic
The data comes in pairs, which means each subject has exactly two measurements that are linked. For example:

The same patient measured before and after treatment
The same clinic’s performance in January vs. June
Twins where one receives treatment and the other serves as control



Why Use Paired Data?
The paired design is statistically more powerful than an independent design because it eliminates the variability across respondents. For example, if we compare pain scores between a treatment group and control group (independent design), differences in pain tolerance between individuals add noise to our data. But if we measure each person’s pain before and after treatment (paired design), individual differences cancel out, and we are only looking at how much each person’s pain perceptions changed.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
When to Use It
The paired-samples t-test is appropriate whenever your measurements are somehow related:

Before-and-after studies (same respondent):

Pre-treatment vs. post-treatment outcomes
Before vs. after policy implementation
Baseline vs. follow-up measurements

Matched pairs design:

Twin studies (comparing outcomes between twins)
Matched control studies (subjects paired on key characteristics)

Within-subject comparisons:

Two treatments tested on the same patient (crossover design)
Morning vs. evening measurements on the same individuals
Left eye vs. right eye comparisons

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
section: Paired-Samples t-test Scenario: Pain Management Protocol
text:
Paired-Samples t-test Scenario: Pain Management Protocol
A hospital implemented a new non-pharmacological pain management protocol (integrating guided imagery and music therapy) and wants to evaluate its effectiveness. Rather than comparing different groups of patients (which would introduce confounding variables like age, health status, or pain tolerance), the hospital measures pain scores (0-10 scale) for 30 patients before and after receiving the protocol.
The key question is: Did the protocol significantly reduce pain?
By using the same patients as their own controls, we can isolate the effect of the protocol from individual differences in pain perception and tolerance.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
Hypotheses
For our pain management protocol evaluation:

Null Hypothesis (H₀): μ_D = 0 (The mean difference in pain scores is zero—no change)
Alternative Hypothesis (H₁): μ_D ≠ 0 (The mean difference is not zero—pain scores changed)

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
The Formula
The paired t-test analyzes the differences between paired observations:
\[t = \frac{\bar{D}}{s_D / \sqrt{n}}\]
Where:

\(\bar{D}\): mean of the differences (average change across all subjects)
\(s_D\): standard deviation of the differences (variability in how much individuals changed)
\(n\): number of pairs (number of subjects)


Understanding the Formula
Notice that this formula is essentially identical to the one-sample t-test formula! This is because the paired t-test is really just a one-sample t-test performed on the differences. We’re testing whether the mean difference is significantly different from zero.
Instead of working with two sets of measurements (e.g., average before - average after), we first calculate the difference for each pair (e.g., Before - After for each patient). Then we examine whether the average of these differences significantly different from zero.

If the mean difference is close to zero → no significant difference
If the mean difference is far from zero (relative to variability) → significant difference

This approach is powerful because it accounts for individual baseline differences. A patient who starts with severe pain and a patient who starts with mild pain are compared only to themselves.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests

What is a One-Sample t-test?
A one-sample t-test compares a sample mean to a known or hypothesized population mean or value.

 Key Question: Is our sample mean significantly different from a benchmark?


 Key Components:

One group of observations (your sample data)
One comparison value (a known or hypothesized population mean, benchmark, standard, or target)

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
text:
When to Use It
The one-sample t-test is appropriate when comparing against a fixed reference:

Performance vs. industry benchmarks (e.g., length of stay vs. national average)
Outcomes vs. target levels (e.g., satisfaction scores vs. target of 8.0)
Metrics vs. regulatory requirements (e.g., readmission rates vs. CMS standards)

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
section: One-Sample t-test Scenario:  Emergency Department Waiting Times
text:
One-Sample t-test Scenario:  Emergency Department Waiting Times

Imagine you are an administrator at a hospital where the regional average emergency department waiting time is 45 minutes.



Recently, you’ve received complaints that patients are waiting too long. To investigate, you randomly sample 30 patients and record their waiting times.




The key question:

Is this difference statistically significant, or could it simply be due to natural variation in the data?

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
section: A Quick Review of Null Hypothesis Testing
text:
A Quick Review of Null Hypothesis Testing


Two competing explanations for the difference:

Explanation 1 (H1): The hospital’s mean waiting time is longer than 45 minutes
Explanation 2 (H₀): The hospital’s mean waiting time is 45 minutes (but coincidentally, the sample mean is higher than 45 minutes)

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
text:
Hypotheses
For our ED waiting times scenario:

Null Hypothesis (H₀): μ = 45 (The hospital’s mean waiting time equals the 45-minute regional standard)
Alternative Hypothesis (H₁): μ ≠ 45 (The hospital’s mean waiting time differs from the standard)


The t-test will help us decide whether to reject H₀ based on our sample data.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
text:
The Formula
The t-statistic is calculated as:
\[t = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt{n}}\]

Where:

\(\bar{X}\): sample mean (e.g., 52 minutes in our scenario)
\(\mu_0\): hypothesized/known mean (e.g., 45-minute benchmark)
\(s\): sample standard deviation (measures the spread of your data)
\(n\): sample size (e.g., 30 patients in our scenario)

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
text:
Understanding the Formula
Numerator (\(\bar{X} - \mu_0\)):

The difference between observed and expected under the null hypothesis


Denominator (\(s / \sqrt{n}\)):

The standard error of the mean
Tells us expected variability in sample means



Interpretation:

t ≈ 0 → sample mean close to benchmark
|t| large → sample mean far from benchmark

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
section: Demonstration:  Extract the Data and Calculation
text:
Demonstration:  Extract the Data and Calculation

# Extract ED waiting times from our dataset
waiting_times <- hospital_ops$ed_wait_time # getting wait time data
mu_0 <- 45  # benchmark (regional average)
n <- length(waiting_times) # sample size
x_bar <- mean(waiting_times) # sample mean
s <- sd(waiting_times) # sample standard deviation
se <- s / sqrt(n) # standard error of the mean
t_stat <- (x_bar - mu_0) / se # t-statistic


Our t-statistic (2.52) tells us how many standard errors our sample mean is from the benchmark.

df (29): Degrees of freedom (n - 1)

text:
Interpreting the Results
Key findings:

The p-value is less than 0.05, so we reject the null hypothesis — the observed difference is unlikely due to chance alone
The 45-minute benchmark is NOT within the 95% confidence interval, which further confirms that the true mean is significantly different from 45
Conclusion: The evidence strongly suggests that the hospital’s average ED waiting time is significantly higher than the 45-minute regional standard

Need to investigate causes and potential interventions for the longer wait times.

What is an Independent-Samples t-test?

text:
When to Use It
The independent-samples t-test is appropriate when comparing two separate, independent groups:

Comparing treatments: New drug vs. standard treatment
Comparing facilities: One hospital vs. another (Hospital A vs. Hospital B)
Intervention studies: Intervention group vs. control group
Demographic comparisons: Urban vs. rural outcomes

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
section: Independent-Samples t-test Scenario:  Comparing Intake Systems
text:
Independent-Samples t-test Scenario:  Comparing Intake Systems
Situation: Your health system is considering digital intake systems.

Hospital A: Digital tablet-based intake
Hospital B: Traditional paper forms


 Question: Does the digital system result in faster processing times?


 You collect processing time data from 15 randomly selected patients at each hospital to determine whether the difference represents a real efficiency gain.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
text:
Hypotheses
For our intake systems comparison:

Null Hypothesis (H₀): μ₁ = μ₂ (Mean processing time is the same for both systems)
Alternative Hypothesis (H₁): μ₁ ≠ μ₂ (Mean processing times differ between systems)


The t-test will help us decide whether the observed difference is statistically significant.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
text:
The Formula
\[t = \frac{\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2}{s_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}}\]

Pooled standard deviation:
\[s_p = \sqrt{\frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2 + (n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}}\]

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
text:
Understanding the Formula
Numerator (\(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\)):

The difference between the two sample means


Denominator:

Standard error of the difference between means
Combines variability from both groups



Pooled SD (\(s_p\)):

Weighted average of both groups’ SDs
Assumes equal population variances

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
text:
Demonstration: Extract the Data
First, let’s get each hospital’s intake time data.

# Extract data from our dataset
hospital_A <- hospital_ops$intake_time[hospital_ops$intake_hospital == "A_Digital"]
hospital_B <- hospital_ops$intake_time[hospital_ops$intake_hospital == "B_Paper"]

Let’s check descriptive statistics for each hospital.

# Hospital A: Digital 
mean(hospital_A) # average intake time in minutes
sd(hospital_A)   # standard deviation of intake time in minutes
length(hospital_A) # number of patients

# Hospital B: Paper
mean(hospital_B) # average intake time in minutes
sd(hospital_B)   # standard deviation of intake time in minutes
length(hospital_B) # number of patients

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
text:
Visualizing Group Differences


Code
# Create grouped data for visualization
intake_viz <- hospital_ops %>%
  mutate(hospital_label = ifelse(intake_hospital == "A_Digital", 
                                  "A: Digital System", "B: Paper Forms"))

# Box plot with individual points
ggplot(intake_viz, aes(x = hospital_label, y = intake_time, fill = hospital_label)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, width = 0.4) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  labs(title = "Patient Intake Processing Times by System",
       subtitle = "Comparing digital (A) vs. paper (B) intake systems",
       x = "Hospital System", y = "Processing Time (minutes)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
text:
Demonstration: Using t.test() in R
Same as one-sample t-test, we can use t.test() function in R.

# Perform independent samples t-test
# var.equal = TRUE uses pooled variance (Student's t-test)
result_ind <- t.test(hospital_A, hospital_B, var.equal = TRUE)
# alternatively: t.test(intake_time ~ intake_hospital, data = hospital_ops, var.equal = TRUE)
parameters(result_ind)

Two Sample t-test

Parameter1 | Parameter2 | Mean_Parameter1 | Mean_Parameter2 | Difference
------------------------------------------------------------------------
hospital_A | hospital_B |           14.53 |           16.53 |      -2.00

Parameter1 |         95% CI | t(28) |      p
--------------------------------------------
hospital_A | [-3.11, -0.89] | -3.70 | < .001

Alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
text:
Components of the Output

t-statistic (-3.7): Distance between the two group means in SE units
df (28): Degrees of freedom (n₁ + n₂ - 2)
p-value (0.00094): Probability of seeing this or more extreme result if null is true
95% CI [-3.11, -0.89]: Range for the true difference in means

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
text:
Interpreting the Results
Key findings:

The p-value is less than 0.05, so we reject the null hypothesis — the observed difference between the two groups is unlikely due to chance alone
Zero is NOT within the 95% confidence interval, which further confirms that the true difference in means is significantly different from zero
Conclusion: The digital intake system (Hospital A) has significantly shorter processing times than the paper system (Hospital B)

This supports investing in digital intake systems across the health system.

text:

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
text:
What is a Paired-Samples t-test?
A paired-samples t-test compares two related measurements on the same subjects.

 Key Question: Is there a significant change within the same individuals?


 Key Characteristic:

Data comes in pairs (each subject/patient has two linked measurements)

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
text:
Why Use Paired Data?
Key Advantage: Each person serves as their own control!

Eliminates variability between individuals
Increases statistical power to detect true effects
More efficient use of data

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
text:
When to Use It
The paired-samples t-test is appropriate for related measurements:

Before-and-after studies: Pre-treatment vs. post-treatment
Matched pairs: Twins, matched controls
Within-subject comparisons: Two conditions on the same patient

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
section: Paired-Samples t-test Scenario:  Pain Management Protocol
text:
Paired-Samples t-test Scenario:  Pain Management Protocol
Situation: A hospital implemented a new non-pharmacological pain management protocol (integrating guided imagery and music therapy).

 To evaluate effectiveness, they measure pain scores (0-10 scale) for 30 patients before and after the protocol.


 Question: Did the protocol significantly reduce pain?

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
text:
Hypotheses
For our pain management protocol evaluation:

Null Hypothesis (H₀): μ_D = 0 (The mean difference in pain scores is zero — no change)
Alternative Hypothesis (H₁): μ_D ≠ 0 (The mean difference is not zero — pain scores changed)


The t-test will help us determine whether the protocol had a significant effect.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
text:
The Formula
The paired t-test analyzes differences between paired observations:
\[t = \frac{\bar{D}}{s_D / \sqrt{n}}\]

Where:

\(\bar{D}\): mean of the differences
\(s_D\): standard deviation of the differences
\(n\): number of pairs

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
text:
Paired-Samples t-test Demonstration
Let’s first get the pain scores from our dataset.

# Extract pain scores from our dataset
before <- hospital_ops$pain_before
after <- hospital_ops$pain_after
differences <- before - after

Let’s check descriptive statistics of the pain scores.

# Before Treatment 
mean(before)
sd(before)

# After Treatment
mean(after)
sd(after)

# Before - After
mean(differences)
sd(differences)

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
text:
Visualizing Paired Data


Code
pain_data <- data.frame(
  patient = rep(1:30, 2),
  time = factor(rep(c("Before", "After"), each = 30),
                levels = c("Before", "After")),
  score = c(before, after)
)

ggplot(pain_data, aes(x = time, y = score, group = patient)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3, color = "gray30") +
  geom_point(aes(color = time), size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  stat_summary(aes(group = 1), fun = mean, geom = "line",
               linewidth = 2, color = "red") +
  stat_summary(aes(group = 1), fun = mean, geom = "point",
               size = 4, color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Individual Patient Pain Scores",
       subtitle = "Red line shows mean change",
       x = "", y = "Pain Score (0-10)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
text:
Interpreting the Paired Plot

Gray lines: Individual patient changes (some improved, some didn’t)
Red line: Overall mean change
Downward slope: Average pain decreased after treatment

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
text:
Demonstration: Using t.test() in R
Same as other t-tests, we can use t.test() function with paired = TRUE option.

# Perform paired samples t-test
result_paired <- t.test(before, after, paired = TRUE)
parameters(result_paired)

Paired t-test

Parameter | Group | Difference | t(29) |     p |       95% CI
-------------------------------------------------------------
before    | after |       0.40 |  2.84 | 0.008 | [0.11, 0.69]

Alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
text:
Components of the Output

t-statistic (2.84): Distance of the mean difference from zero in SE units
df (29): Degrees of freedom (n - 1)
p-value (0.0081): Probability of seeing this or more extreme result if null is true
95% CI [0.11, 0.69]: Range for the true mean difference

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-tests
text:
Interpreting the Results
Key findings:

The p-value is less than 0.05, so we reject the null hypothesis — the observed change in pain scores is unlikely due to chance alone
Zero is NOT within the 95% confidence interval, which further confirms that the true mean difference is significantly different from zero
Conclusion: The non-pharmacological pain management protocol significantly reduced pain scores

This supports expanding the protocol to other departments or patient populations.

text:
Decision Flowchart
Use this guide to select the appropriate t-test:









Question
If Yes…
R Function




Comparing to a benchmark?
One-sample
t.test(x, mu = value)


Two separate groups?
Independent-samples
t.test(x, y, var.equal = TRUE)


Same subjects, twice?

“Do patients at Hospital A have shorter stays than Hospital B?” → Independent-samples
“Did patient satisfaction improve after our intervention?” → Paired-samples

text:

One-sample t-tests: Evaluate if you meet standards or benchmarks
Independent-samples t-tests: Compare different treatments, departments, or facilities
Paired-samples t-tests: Evaluate effectiveness of interventions
All t-tests: Use t.test() in R with appropriate arguments

title: Basic Statistical Concepts (Lecture Notes)
text:
Imagine you are presenting to your hospital’s board: “Our average patient satisfaction score is 5.2 out of 7.” A board member asks, “Is that good? How does it compare to last quarter? Are all departments performing similarly?”
Without understanding central tendency, dispersion, and how to interpret differences, you might misrepresent your data, or worse, make decisions based on misleading numbers. This lecture gives you the tools to answer these questions confidently.
As a healthcare manager, you make decisions daily that affect:

Patient outcomes: Quality of care, safety, satisfaction
Operational efficiency: Staffing, resource allocation, workflow
Financial performance: Cost management, budget planning
Strategic planning: Service line development, capacity planning

Understanding basic statistical concepts helps you:

Describe your data accurately (What’s typical? How much variation exists?)
Compare groups meaningfully (Are these differences real or random?)
Make evidence-based decisions (What does the data actually say?)
Communicate findings clearly to diverse stakeholders
