title: Penalized Regression in Healthcare Analytics (Lecture Notes)
text:
2.1 Review: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) Regression
Before diving into penalized methods, let’s recall how standard linear regression works. This review will help us understand what we’re modifying and why.

2.1.1 The Basic Setup
In linear regression, we want to predict a continuous outcome variable \(Y\) (e.g., healthcare costs) using a set of predictor variables \(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_p\) (e.g., age, diagnoses, prior utilization). We assume the relationship takes the form:
\[\hat{Y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \cdots + \beta_p X_p\]
Where:

\(\hat{Y}\) is our predicted value
\(\beta_0\) is the intercept (predicted value when all X’s are zero)
\(\beta_1, \beta_2, \ldots, \beta_p\) are coefficients that tell us how much \(Y\) changes for a one-unit change in each predictor

Note on terminology: Throughout this document, we use the terms “predictor,” “variable,” and “feature” interchangeably to refer to the X variables used to predict the outcome.


2.1.2 How OLS Finds the Best Coefficients
OLS finds the coefficient values that minimize the Sum of Squared Errors (SSE), the total squared difference between what we predicted and what actually happened:
\[\text{Minimize: } SSE = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)^2\]
We square the prediction errors (so positive and negative errors don’t cancel out), add them up across all observations, and find the intercept and coefficients that make this sum as small as possible.
This approach works excellently when:

We have many more observations than predictors (\(n >> p\))
Predictors are not highly correlated with each other
Our primary goal is to understand relationships (statistical inference)

However, modern healthcare analytics often violates these conditions, leading to several major problems.

title: Penalized Regression in Healthcare Analytics (Lecture Notes)
section: 2.2 Problems with Standard Regression in Healthcare
text:
2.2 Problems with Standard Regression in Healthcare

Related variables create confusion


Healthcare factors naturally cluster together. For example, diabetes patients often have high blood pressure and obesity, patients with many doctor visits also have many prescriptions, etc.
When variables are related, standard regression can’t determine which one truly drives the outcome. This leads to unstable results: coefficients can become wildly inflated, have wrong signs, or change dramatically with small data changes.


Too many variables, too few observations


Healthcare data often has hundreds of potential predictors (diagnosis codes, medications, lab tests) but limited patients. For example, a hospital might have 300 patients but 250 potential predictor variables (or even more predictors than patients)
The result: the model “memorizes” your specific patients rather than learning general patterns (overfitting). It predicts your current patients perfectly but fails miserably on new patients.


Hard to identify what factors are really important


Standard regression uses every variable you give it, even irrelevant ones. You end up with all hundreds of variables in your model.
Healthcare organizations need interpretable, actionable models (clinicians can’t use hundreds of factors to make decisions).

title: Penalized Regression in Healthcare Analytics (Lecture Notes)
text:
2.3 The Solution: Penalized Regression

2.3.1 The Key Insight
Those problems above stem from too much flexibility (meaning OLS can set coefficients to any value to minimize training error). A potential solution is to constrain the coefficients, preventing them from becoming too large.
We do this by modifying the OLS objective function:
\[\text{Minimize: } SSE + \lambda \times \text{Penalty}\]
In plain language, find coefficients that balance [prediction accuracy] + [penalty for model complexity]
Where:

SSE = Sum of Squared Errors (how well the model fits the training data)
Penalty = A function of the coefficient sizes (how complex the model is)
λ (lambda) = A tuning parameter that controls how much we penalize complexity



2.3.2 How the Penalty Helps
Why does the penalty improve predictions? Without constraints, standard regression overfits—it “memorizes” the quirks of your specific patients rather than learning general patterns. The penalty prevents this by keeping the model simple enough to work well on new patients. Think of it like studying concepts versus memorizing answers: concepts work on new problems, memorization doesn’t.
The penalty term creates a tradeoff:

Making SSE smaller (better fit) typically requires larger, more complex coefficients
Making the penalty smaller requires smaller coefficients
The optimal solution balances these competing goals: slightly worse fit on your current data in exchange for better predictions on new patients

How this addresses each problem:

Handles correlated variables: When variables are related (like diabetes, obesity, and blood pressure), the penalty prevents coefficients from becoming wildly inflated.
Prevents overfitting with many variables: The penalty stops the model from “memorizing” your specific patients. By shrinking coefficients, it forces the model to focus only on the strongest, most reliable patterns that will generalize to new patients.
Automatic variable selection (LASSO): The L1 penalty pushes weak predictors to exactly zero, eliminating them from the model entirely. You end up with a small set of important variables instead of hundreds.



2.3.3 The Role of Lambda (λ)
The tuning parameter λ controls how much we care about the penalty:

λ = 0: No penalty, model equals OLS
Small λ: Light penalty, close to OLS
Large λ: Heavy penalty, coefficients shrunk toward zero
λ → ∞: All coefficients forced to zero (except intercept)

We need to choose λ carefully (too small and we don’t solve our problems; too large and we throw away useful information). We’ll discuss how to select λ using cross-validation later.

title: Penalized Regression in Healthcare Analytics (Lecture Notes)
text:
3.1 Ridge Regression: The L2 Penalty
Now let’s examine the first specific type of penalized regression: Ridge regression. This method addresses multicollinearity and overfitting by shrinking all coefficients toward zero.

3.1.1 Mathematical Formulation
Ridge regression adds a penalty based on the squared values of coefficients:
\[\text{Minimize: } \sum_{i=1}^{n} (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p} \beta_j^2\]
The penalty term \(\sum_{j=1}^{p} \beta_j^2\) is called the L2 penalty or squared penalty because we’re summing squared coefficients.
What this formula says:
“Find the coefficients that make predictions accurate (small SSE) while also keeping coefficients small (small sum of squared betas). The parameter λ controls how much we care about keeping coefficients small.”


3.1.2 How Ridge Regression Works
Ridge regression works by gently discouraging large coefficients. Instead of allowing the model to rely too heavily on any single predictor, it nudges all coefficients toward smaller values. This has several important consequences.

Ridge regression shrinks all coefficients toward zero, but does not remove variables.

As the penalty becomes stronger, coefficient values get smaller and smaller. However, they do not drop all the way to zero. This means Ridge regression keeps all predictors in the model, but limits how strongly each one can influence the outcome.

Larger coefficients are shrunk more than smaller ones.

Ridge regression is especially uncomfortable with very large coefficients. If one predictor has a much larger effect than others, the penalty pushes it down more strongly. Smaller coefficients are affected less. This helps prevent the model from overreacting to noise or peculiarities in the data.

Ridge regression handles correlated predictors smoothly.

When predictors are highly correlated, ordinary regression often struggles to decide which one deserves credit, leading to unstable or counterintuitive estimates. Ridge regression avoids this problem by sharing the effect across correlated variables. Instead of picking one variable and inflating its coefficient, it assigns moderate coefficients to both, producing more sensible and reliable results.


3.1.3 Visual Understanding: The Constraint Region
One of the best ways to understand Ridge regression is geometrically. Imagine we have just two predictors, so we’re looking for β₁ and β₂.



LASSO and Ridge Penalty


Understanding the figure:

Red ellipses: Contour lines of SSE. The center is where SSE is minimized (the OLS solution). Moving away from the center increases SSE.
Blue shaded region: The constraint region - all combinations of β₁ and β₂ that satisfy the penalty constraint. For Ridge, this is a circle because we’re constraining \(\beta_1^2 + \beta_2^2 \leq c\) (equation of a circle).
The solution: We want to be as close to the OLS center as possible (small SSE) while staying within the constraint region (small penalty). The Ridge solution is where the (smallest) ellipse touches the circle.

Key insight: Because the constraint region is a circle, the solution rarely lands exactly on an axis. This means Ridge keeps all variables with non-zero coefficients.


3.1.4 Advantages of Ridge Regression
1. Handles correlated predictors well
When predictors overlap heavily, Ridge regression avoids extreme or unstable estimates. Instead of forcing the model to “choose sides,” it spreads influence across related variables in a balanced way.
2. Reduces coefficient instability from multicollinearity
When predictors are correlated, ordinary regression produces unstable coefficient estimates that can change dramatically with small data changes. Ridge regression stabilizes these estimates by limiting how large they can grow.
3. Improves prediction accuracy on new data
By preventing overfitting to training data, Ridge regression often achieves better prediction performance on new, unseen patients compared to ordinary regression.
4. Keeps all relevant information
If most predictors are believed to matter at least a little, Ridge regression retains them all while preventing any single variable from dominating.


3.1.5 Disadvantages of Ridge Regression
1. Does not simplify the model
Ridge regression keeps every predictor in the model. When there are many variables, this can make the model hard to summarize or deploy.
2. Limited interpretability
Because effects are spread across many small coefficients, it is difficult to identify which predictors are truly important. Ridge is better suited for prediction than explanation.
3. Retains noisy predictors
Variables with no real signal are not removed, only weakened. When many such variables are present, their combined influence can reduce performance.


3.1.6 When to Use Ridge Regression
Ridge regression is best when:

Predictors are strongly correlated
Most variables are expected to carry some information
Prediction is the main goal (interpretation is less important)
The number of predictors is moderate rather than very large

title: Penalized Regression in Healthcare Analytics (Lecture Notes)
text:
3.2 LASSO Regression: The L1 Penalty
LASSO (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator) is the other major penalized regression method. Its key advantage over Ridge is automatic feature selection: LASSO can eliminate variables entirely by setting their coefficients exactly to zero.

3.2.1 Mathematical Formulation
LASSO adds a penalty based on the absolute values of coefficients:
\[\text{Minimize: } \sum_{i=1}^{n} (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p} |\beta_j|\]
The penalty term \(\sum_{j=1}^{p} |\beta_j|\) is called the L1 penalty or absolute value penalty.
The critical difference from Ridge is that LASSO uses absolute values instead of squared values, which changes the geometry in a way that allows coefficients to become exactly zero.


3.2.2 How LASSO Achieves Feature Selection
LASSO’s key feature selection property comes from its constraint shape (see the figure above). The LASSO constraint has sharp corners along the axes. When the model searches for the best fit, it often lands on one of these corners—where one or more coefficients are exactly zero.
In contrast, Ridge regression uses a smooth, round constraint. This makes it unlikely for coefficients to be driven all the way to zero, so all predictors remain in the model.


3.2.3 Advantages of LASSO Regression
1. Automatic feature selection
LASSO identifies a small set of important predictors and removes the rest, making it especially useful when many variables are available but only some are informative.
2. Interpretability
With fewer active predictors, the model’s logic is easier to understand and explain in practical terms.
3. Effective in high-dimensional settings
LASSO works even when the number of predictors exceeds the number of observations, which is common with diagnostic codes, procedures, or lab measures.
4. Controls overfitting
By excluding noisy predictors, LASSO reduces the risk of capturing patterns that do not generalize.


3.2.4 Disadvantages of LASSO Regression
1. Unstable with correlated predictors
When predictors are highly correlated, LASSO tends to select one and drop the others. Which variable is chosen can vary across samples, making interpretation fragile.
2. May discard useful information
By setting coefficients exactly to zero, LASSO can remove predictors that still carry some signal. In purely predictive tasks, Ridge may perform slightly better.
3. Selection is limited in very small samples
When the sample size is small, LASSO can only select a limited number of predictors, potentially missing relevant factors.


3.2.5 When to Use LASSO Regression
LASSO is best when:

Identifying key predictors is a primary goal
Simplicity and interpretability matters
You have many potential predictors and need feature selection
Predictors are not highly correlated

title: Penalized Regression in Healthcare Analytics (Lecture Notes)
text:
3.3 Elastic Net
Elastic Net combines the strengths of both Ridge and LASSO by using both penalties together. It’s often the best choice in practice because it handles correlated variables better than LASSO while still performing feature selection.

3.3.1 Mathematical Formulation
Elastic Net minimizes:
\[\text{Minimize: } \sum_{i=1}^{n} (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)^2 + \lambda \left[ \alpha \sum_{j=1}^{p} |\beta_j| + (1-\alpha) \sum_{j=1}^{p} \beta_j^2 \right]\]
Where:

α (alpha) controls the mix of L1 and L2 penalties
α = 1: Pure LASSO
α = 0: Pure Ridge
0 < α < 1: Elastic Net blend



3.3.2 How Elastic Net Handles Correlated Variables
When predictors are strongly correlated, LASSO tends to select one and discard the rest, even if they all carry meaningful information. Ridge takes the opposite approach, keeping everything and shrinking coefficients together. Elastic Net sits between these two.
The key idea is the grouping effect. Elastic Net tends to keep or remove groups of related variables together, rather than making arbitrary choices among them. The Ridge component encourages correlated predictors to stay together, while the LASSO component removes predictors (or groups) that contribute little to prediction.
For example, imagine you include several variables that capture a patient’s overall health status in different ways (e.g., past diagnoses, prior hospital use, overall medical complexity, etc.) along with many unrelated predictors.

LASSO might keep one of these health measures and drop others
Ridge would keep all measures, including many irrelevant ones
Elastic Net would likely keep all of the health measures together, while removing unrelated noise variables



3.3.3 Tuning Elastic Net
Elastic Net balances two competing goals: simplicity and stability. It uses two parameters two control this balance.

λ (lambda): How strongly coefficients are penalized overall
α (alpha): How much the model behaves like LASSO vs. Ridge

In practice, the model tries different balances and selects the one that performs best on new data. Rather than committing to LASSO or Ridge upfront, Elastic Net lets the data decide how much feature selection and how much stabilization are needed.


3.3.4 Advantages of Elastic Net

Combines feature selection and stability

Elastic Net can remove unimportant predictors while keeping correlated, meaningful ones together.

More stable than LASSO

When predictors overlap, Elastic Net produces more consistent selections across samples, reducing the risk of arbitrary choices.

Effective in very high dimensions

Unlike LASSO, Elastic Net can retain more predictors when the number of variables far exceeds the number of observations.

Highly adaptable

By adjusting the balance between LASSO and Ridge, Elastic Net can be tailored to different data structures and research goals.


3.3.5 Disadvantages of Elastic Net

More tuning required

Elastic Net introduces an extra decision (parameter) compared to Ridge or LASSO, which significantly increases complexity.

Same modeling assumptions as linear regression

Elastic Net improves estimation and selection, but it does not address nonlinearity or misspecified relationships.

Not always necessary

If predictors are largely independent, LASSO alone may suffice. If feature selection is unnecessary, Ridge alone may be simpler.


3.3.6 When to Use Elastic Net
Elastic Net is often a strong default choice, especially when:

Predictors are correlated and feature selection is desired
You are not sure whether Ridge or LASSO is more appropriate
The data are high-dimensional
Stability in selected predictors matters

Elastic Net is often the best starting choice because it combines Ridge’s stability with LASSO’s feature selection. If you’re unsure which method to use, start with Elastic Net and let cross-validation determine the optimal balance between Ridge and LASSO.

Low (many variables)
High (sparse model)
Moderate


Best for
Correlated predictors, all relevant
Feature selection, uncorrelated
General use, correlated with selection

title: Penalized Regression in Healthcare Analytics (Lecture Notes)
text:
3.5 Choosing Lambda: Cross-Validation
We need to choose the right λ value, but how?
The challenge: We can’t just pick the λ that works best on our current patients. That would be like a student memorizing practice test answers. We need to know which λ will work best on new patients we haven’t seen yet.
The solution: Cross-validation
Think of cross-validation as creating multiple “practice tests”:

Divide your data into 10 groups (called “folds”; the number of groups can vary)
For each λ value you want to try:

Train the model on 9 groups, test on the 10th group
Repeat 10 times, each time holding out a different group
Average the prediction errors across all 10 tests

Pick the λ with the lowest average error

Why this works: Every patient gets used for both training AND testing (just not at the same time). This efficiently uses all your data to estimate how well each λ will perform on new patients.
In practice: The software (like R’s glmnet package) does this automatically. You’ll see which λ performs best, and we’ll discuss how to interpret the results in the hands-on section.

title: Penalized Regression in Healthcare Analytics (Lecture Notes)
section: 4.1 The Case: Predicting Patient Healthcare Costs
text:
4.1 The Case: Predicting Patient Healthcare Costs
Problem:
Imagine you work for a health insurance company. Every year, your company needs to predict how much each patient will cost in healthcare spending so you can:

Set appropriate insurance premiums
Budget for the coming year
Identify high-cost patients who might benefit from care management programs (like helping diabetics control their blood sugar to avoid expensive complications)

Your Task:
Build a model that predicts next year’s total healthcare spending for each patient based on information you currently have about them.
Available Data:
You have data on 500 patients, including:

Demographics: Age, sex
Socioeconomic factors: Income level, insurance status
Health behaviors: Smoking, BMI, exercise frequency
Chronic conditions: Diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; a chronic lung disease), depression, arthritis
Prior healthcare use: Emergency room visits, hospitalizations, doctor visits, number of medications
Outcome variable is annual healthcare cost (the total cost of care; the insurance company pays out to hospitals, doctors, and other healthcare providers for a patient’s care over a year).

The Challenge:
With so many potential predictors (some of which are related to each other), standard regression may struggle. We’ll use penalized regression to build a model that predicts well on new patients.

title: Penalized Regression in Healthcare Analytics (Lecture Notes)
section: 4.2 Creating a Healthcare Cost Prediction Dataset
text:
4.2 Creating a Healthcare Cost Prediction Dataset
For this tutorial, we’ll create a realistic simulated dataset representing this scenario.


Code
# Number of patients in our dataset
n <- 500

# Generate patient characteristics
healthcare_data <- data.frame(
  patient_id = 1:n,

  # Demographics
  age = round(rnorm(n, mean = 55, sd = 15)),
  female = rbinom(n, 1, 0.52),

  # Socioeconomic factors
  income_level = sample(1:5, n, replace = TRUE,
                        prob = c(0.15, 0.20, 0.30, 0.20, 0.15)),
  has_insurance = rbinom(n, 1, 0.88),

  # Health behaviors
  smoker = rbinom(n, 1, 0.18),
  bmi = round(rnorm(n, mean = 28, sd = 6), 1),
  exercise_days = rpois(n, lambda = 2),

  # Chronic conditions - these will be major cost drivers
  diabetes = rbinom(n, 1, 0.12),
  hypertension = rbinom(n, 1, 0.30),
  heart_disease = rbinom(n, 1, 0.08),
  copd = rbinom(n, 1, 0.06),
  depression = rbinom(n, 1, 0.15),
  arthritis = rbinom(n, 1, 0.22),

  # Healthcare utilization from prior year
  ed_visits = rpois(n, lambda = 0.5),
  hospitalizations = rpois(n, lambda = 0.15),
  physician_visits = rpois(n, lambda = 4),
  num_medications = rpois(n, lambda = 3)
)

# Make chronic conditions more realistic by adding correlations
healthcare_data <- healthcare_data %>%
  mutate(
    diabetes = ifelse(bmi > 30 & age > 50,
                      rbinom(n(), 1, 0.25), diabetes),
    hypertension = ifelse(diabetes == 1,
                          rbinom(n(), 1, 0.65), hypertension),
    heart_disease = ifelse(diabetes == 1 & hypertension == 1 & age > 60,
                           rbinom(n(), 1, 0.30), heart_disease)
  )

# Generate the outcome variable: Annual healthcare costs
healthcare_data <- healthcare_data %>%
  mutate(
    annual_cost =
      # Base cost
      2000 +
      # Demographics
      age * 50 +
      (1 - has_insurance) * 1500 +
      # Health behaviors
      smoker * 2000 +
      pmax(bmi - 25, 0) * 100 +
      # Chronic conditions
      diabetes * 5000 +
      hypertension * 2000 +
      heart_disease * 8000 +
      copd * 6000 +
      depression * 1500 +
      arthritis * 1000 +
      # Prior utilization
      ed_visits * 1500 +
      hospitalizations * 15000 +
      physician_visits * 200 +
      num_medications * 500 +
      # Random noise
      rnorm(n(), 0, 3000)
  ) %>%
  mutate(annual_cost = pmax(annual_cost, 500))

text:
4.3 Data Preparation for glmnet
Before we can use penalized regression, we need to prepare our data in a specific format and split it into training and test sets.
Let’s use 70% of the data to build the model (training set) and 30% to evaluate how well the model predicts on new patients (test set; data not used for training the model). Within the training set, we perform 10-fold cross-validation to choose λ.

# Split into training (70%) and test (30%) sets
train_index <- sample(1:n, size = 0.7 * n)
train_data <- healthcare_data[train_index, ] # Training Dataset
test_data <- healthcare_data[-train_index, ] # Test Dataset

# Define predictor variables
predictor_vars <- setdiff(names(healthcare_data), c("patient_id", "annual_cost"))

# Create matrix format required by glmnet
x_train <- as.matrix(train_data[, predictor_vars])
y_train <- train_data$annual_cost

x_test <- as.matrix(test_data[, predictor_vars])
y_test <- test_data$annual_cost

Our dataset now contains 350 patients (70%) in the training set and 150 (30%) in the test set. We have 17 predictor variables (age, sex, income, insurance status, health behaviors, chronic conditions, and prior healthcare use).
Note: The glmnet package requires predictors in matrix format (not a data frame) and automatically standardizes them before fitting.

title: Penalized Regression in Healthcare Analytics (Lecture Notes)
text:
4.5 Ridge Regression
Now let’s fit a Ridge regression model using the L2 penalty.

4.5.1 Fitting the Ridge Model

# Fit Ridge regression (alpha = 0)
ridge_model <- glmnet(
  x = x_train,
  y = y_train,
  alpha = 0
)

The glmnet package automatically tests a sequence of lambda values to explore different levels of penalty strength.


4.5.2 Visualizing the Coefficient Paths

# Plot coefficient paths
plot(ridge_model, xvar = "lambda", label = TRUE)
title("Ridge Regression: Coefficient Paths", line = 3)








Interpretation of the plot:

X-axis: -Log(λ) (negative log lambda). Left = large penalty (heavy shrinkage), Right = small penalty (close to OLS)
Y-axis: Coefficient values
Each line: One predictor variable
Key observation: As we move left on the plot (larger λ, stronger penalty), all coefficients shrink toward zero, but none reach exactly zero



4.5.3 Cross-Validation to Find Optimal Lambda
Let’s find an optimal Lambda value by using a cross-validation approach. We will use a 10-fold cross-validation to evaluate different Lambda values and select the one that minimizes the prediction error.

# Perform 10-fold cross-validation
ridge_cv <- cv.glmnet(
  x = x_train,
  y = y_train,
  alpha = 0,
  nfolds = 10 # how many folds will be used
)

# Plot CV results
plot(ridge_cv)
title("Ridge Regression: Cross-Validation Results", line = 3)








The cross-validation plot shows prediction error (vertical axis) for different lambda values (horizontal axis). The two vertical dashed lines mark the two lambda options that cross-validation identifies.
Understanding the two lambda choices:
Cross-validation provides two options:

lambda.min: The λ with the absolute lowest prediction error (best accuracy)
lambda.1se: Uses the “1 standard error rule”: selects the largest λ (simplest model) whose prediction error is within 1 standard error of the minimum. This provides a simpler, more robust model with negligible loss in accuracy.

Let’s use lambda.1se as it is often preferred in practice. It produces simpler models that are less likely to overfit and more likely to generalize well to new patients.

# Extract coefficients at lambda.1se
ridge_coef <- coef(ridge_cv, s = "lambda.1se")

text:
4.6 LASSO Regression
Now let’s fit a LASSO model using the L1 penalty for automatic feature selection.

4.6.1 Fitting the LASSO Model

# Fit LASSO regression (alpha = 1)
lasso_model <- glmnet(
  x = x_train,
  y = y_train,
  alpha = 1
)



4.6.2 Visualizing LASSO Coefficient Paths

# Plot coefficient paths
plot(lasso_model, xvar = "lambda", label = TRUE)
title("LASSO Regression: Coefficient Paths", line = 3)








Key observation: Unlike Ridge, the LASSO paths hit zero! As we move left on the plot (larger λ, stronger penalty), variables are progressively eliminated. This is feature selection.


4.6.3 Cross-Validation for LASSO
Same as our Ridge demonstration, let’s find an optimal lambda value for our LASSO model using a 10-fold cross-validation approach.

# Perform cross-validation
lasso_cv <- cv.glmnet(
  x = x_train,
  y = y_train,
  alpha = 1,
  nfolds = 10
)

# Plot CV results
plot(lasso_cv)
title("LASSO Regression: Cross-Validation Results", line = 3)








The cross-validation plot for LASSO is similar to Ridge, but notice the numbers at the top—they show how many variables remain in the model at each lambda value. As we move left on the plot (larger λ, stronger penalty), LASSO eliminates more variables.


4.6.4 LASSO Feature Selection

title: Penalized Regression in Healthcare Analytics (Lecture Notes)
text:
4.7 Elastic Net Regression
Finally, let’s fit an Elastic Net model that combines Ridge and LASSO penalties.

4.7.1 Tuning Alpha and Lambda
For the alpha parameter (weights of L1 and L2 regularization), we will use a grid search method (starting from 0, we will increase alpha by 0.1 every time).

# Define grid of alpha values
alpha_grid <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.1)

# Store results
elastic_results <- data.frame(
  alpha = alpha_grid,
  lambda_1se = NA,
  mse_1se = NA,
  n_features = NA
)

# Use consistent CV folds (10)
fold_id <- sample(1:10, size = length(y_train), replace = TRUE) 

# Test each alpha value
for (i in seq_along(alpha_grid)) {
  cv_fit <- cv.glmnet(
    x = x_train,
    y = y_train,
    alpha = alpha_grid[i],
    foldid = fold_id # instead of nfolds, we use foldid approach to have the same data in each fold 
  )

  elastic_results$lambda_1se[i] <- cv_fit$lambda.1se
  # Get MSE at lambda.1se
  idx_1se <- which(cv_fit$lambda == cv_fit$lambda.1se)
  elastic_results$mse_1se[i] <- cv_fit$cvm[idx_1se]

  coef_temp <- coef(cv_fit, s = "lambda.1se")
  elastic_results$n_features[i] <- sum(coef_temp != 0) - 1
}

# Display results
elastic_results

The tuning results show the cross-validated MSE for each alpha value (ranging from 0=pure Ridge to 1=pure LASSO). The alpha with the lowest MSE represents the optimal balance between Ridge and LASSO penalties for this dataset (here, when alpha is 0.8).


4.7.2 Visualizing Alpha Tuning











4.7.3 Fit Final Elastic Net Model

# Fit with best alpha
elastic_cv <- cv.glmnet(
  x = x_train,
  y = y_train,
  alpha = best_alpha,
  nfolds = 10
)

# Extract coefficients
elastic_coef <- coef(elastic_cv, s = "lambda.1se")
n_features_elastic <- sum(elastic_coef != 0) - 1

# Make predictions
elastic_pred <- predict(elastic_cv, s = "lambda.1se", newx = x_test)

# Calculate metrics
elastic_mse <- mean((y_test - elastic_pred)^2)
elastic_rmse <- sqrt(elastic_mse)
elastic_rmse

improvement_elastic

Elastic Net combines the strengths of Ridge and LASSO, achieving strong prediction accuracy while performing feature selection. The model uses the optimal alpha value identified through cross-validation.

OLS has the largest coefficients (no shrinkage)
Ridge shrinks all coefficients but keeps them non-zero
LASSO eliminates several variables entirely (zero coefficients)
Elastic Net balances between Ridge and LASSO

title: Penalized Regression in Healthcare Analytics (Lecture Notes)
text:
5.1 When to Use Each Method
Ridge Regression:

Use when you have correlated predictors and want to keep all variables
Best for prediction when you believe most variables are relevant
Handles multicollinearity well
Not suitable when you need feature selection

LASSO Regression:

Use when you need automatic feature selection
Best for interpretability and sparse models
Works well with many potential predictors
Caution with highly correlated predictors (arbitrary selection)

Elastic Net:

Often the best default choice
Combines strengths of Ridge and LASSO
Handles correlated predictors better than LASSO
Performs feature selection like LASSO
Requires tuning two parameters (α and λ)

title: Penalized Regression in Healthcare Analytics (Lecture Notes)
text:
5.2 Cross-Validation Best Practices

Always use cross-validation to select λ (and α for Elastic Net)
Use consistent folds when comparing different α values
Consider lambda.1se for simpler, more interpretable models
Use lambda.min when prediction accuracy is paramount
Check the CV curve - flat regions indicate room for simplification

title: Penalized Regression in Healthcare Analytics (Lecture Notes)
text:
5.3 Important Caveats

Prediction vs. Causation: Penalized regression is for prediction, not causal inference. Selected variables are associated with outcomes, not necessarily causal drivers.
Feature Selection Stability: LASSO selections can be unstable, especially with correlated predictors. Run multiple samples or use Elastic Net.
Clinical Validation: Always validate that selected features make clinical sense. Statistical selection doesn’t guarantee clinical relevance.
Generalizability: Models should be validated on external data from different time periods or institutions.

title: Conjoint Analysis in Healthcare Management
text:
Conjoint analysis is a survey-based statistical technique used to understand how people make decisions when facing trade-offs between multiple attributes of a product or service.
The core idea is simple: in real life, we rarely get everything we want. When choosing a health insurance plan, for example, we might prefer both low premiums AND low deductibles, but plans with low premiums often come with high deductibles. Conjoint analysis helps us understand how people navigate these trade-offs.
The term “conjoint” comes from “considered jointly” (we’re studying how attributes are evaluated together rather than in isolation). This is crucial because asking someone “Do you prefer low cost?” will always get a “yes,” but asking them to choose between a low-cost option with long wait times vs. a high-cost option with short wait times reveals their true priorities.



Healthcare managers face constant decisions about service design:

Insurance plan design: What combination of premium, deductible, and coverage will attract people?
Clinic operations: Should we prioritize shorter wait times or extended hours?
Telehealth services: Do patients value video consultations enough to pay more for them?
Hospital services: What amenities matter most to patients choosing where to receive care?

Conjoint analysis answers these questions by quantifying preferences. Instead of relying on intuition or simple surveys (e.g., “Would you like shorter wait times?”), conjoint analysis reveals how much each feature actually matters when people must make realistic trade-offs.



By using conjoint analysis, we can get several valuable insights:


Part-worth utilities (also called “part-worths” or “utility scores”) are the building blocks of conjoint analysis. They represent the value or satisfaction that a person derives from a specific level of an attribute.
What is “utility”? In this context, “utility” is an economics term meaning satisfaction or value. Think of it as a numeric score representing how much someone values something (Higher utility = more preferred, lower utility = less preferred).
Think of it this way: every product or service is a bundle of attributes. A health insurance plan is a bundle of (premium, deductible, network size, etc.). The total utility (satisfaction) a person gets from a plan is the sum of the part-worth utilities for each attribute level in that plan.
For example, if the part-worth for “Large Network” is +3 and for “Small Network” is 0, then having a large network adds 3 utility units to the overall plan value. These numbers are relative; they represent relative values, not absolute values on their own.



Once we have part-worth utilities, we can calculate how important each attribute is relative to others. This is done by looking at the range of utilities within each attribute (highest level minus lowest level) and comparing these ranges across attributes.
For example, if premium ranges from 0 to 5 utility units and network size ranges from 0 to 2 units, then premium has a larger impact on preferences and is therefore more “important.”



When price or cost is one of the attributes, we can convert utility differences into dollar values. This tells us how much extra a person would be willing to pay for an improvement in another attribute. (Without a price attribute in the study design, WTP cannot be calculated because there is no price coefficient to serve as the conversion rate between utility and dollars)
For example, if people would pay $50 more per month for a large network versus a small network, this helps managers decide whether investing in network expansion is worthwhile.



By knowing the utilities for each attribute level, we can predict what percentage of people would choose one option over another. This is invaluable for forecasting demand and competitive positioning.




In this class, we will cover the two most common conjoint methods:



What respondents do: Rate each profile on a scale (e.g., 1-10)
Analysis approach: Linear regression (OLS)
Advantages: Simple to understand and implement; builds on familiar regression
Limitations: Respondents may rate all options similarly, not revealing true trade-offs





What respondents do: Choose their preferred option from a set
Analysis approach: Multinomial logistic regression
Advantages: Mimics real-world decisions; forces explicit trade-offs
Limitations: Requires more data preparation and more complicated statistical method

Both methods ultimately produce the same types of outputs (part-worths, importance, WTP, market share), but choice-based conjoint is generally preferred in academic research and practice because it better reflects actual decision-making behavior (Louviere et al., 2000).
Now that we understand what conjoint analysis is and why it’s valuable in healthcare management, let’s work through a practical example. We’ll use one comprehensive case study that demonstrates both rating-based and choice-based approaches, allowing us to see how the methods compare and when you might use each one.

title: Conjoint Analysis in Healthcare Management
text:
Context and Background
One of the most studied applications of conjoint analysis in healthcare management is understanding how employees choose health insurance plans during open enrollment periods. This is a high-stakes decision for both employees (who will live with the plan for a year) and employers (who subsidize the plans).
Research has shown that employees often struggle with this decision due to the complexity of plan attributes. Studies by Sinaiko and Hirth (2011) in the Journal of Health Economics found that many employees make “dominated choices” (selecting plans that are objectively worse than alternatives on all dimensions). Understanding which attributes drive choices can help employers design better communication strategies and plan offerings.
Our example uses three key attributes that consistently appear in health plan conjoint studies:









Attribute
Level 1
Level 2
Why It Matters




Monthly Premium
$200
$300
Direct, visible cost paid every month


Annual Deductible
$500
$1,500
Amount paid before insurance kicks in


Network Size
Large
Small
Access to preferred doctors/hospitals



With 3 attributes and 2 levels each, there are \(2^3 = 8\) possible profile combinations (a full factorial design). This is small enough to show every combination to respondents. In practice, when the number of attributes and levels is larger (e.g., 5 attributes × 3 levels = 243 profiles), researchers use a fractional factorial design that presents only a carefully selected subset of profiles.

title: Conjoint Analysis in Healthcare Management
text:
1. Rating-Based Conjoint Analysis

1.1 Conceptual Overview
In rating-based conjoint analysis, we show respondents hypothetical profiles one at a time and ask them to rate how attractive each option is. For example:

Profile 1: Monthly premium $200, Deductible $1,500, Small network How likely would you be to choose this plan? (Rate 1-10)


Profile 2: Monthly premium $300, Deductible $500, Large network How likely would you be to choose this plan? (Rate 1-10)

A respondent might rate Profile 1 as 4/10 and Profile 2 as 7/10.
By collecting ratings for multiple profiles across many respondents, we can use regression analysis to decompose these ratings into the contribution of each attribute. This works because we have systematically varied the attributes across profiles.


1.2 The Statistical Model
Rating-based conjoint uses ordinary least squares (OLS) regression, the same technique you’ve learned in previous courses. The model assumes that a person’s rating is a linear combination of the utilities they assign to each attribute level:
\[\text{Rating} = \beta_0 + \beta_1(\text{Premium}) + \beta_2(\text{Deductible}) + \beta_3(\text{Network}) + \varepsilon\]
Where:

\(\beta_0\) is the intercept (baseline rating)
\(\beta_1, \beta_2, \beta_3\) are the part-worth utilities for each attribute

For continuous attributes like premium, this is the marginal utility per dollar
For categorical attributes like network size, this is the utility difference between levels

\(\varepsilon\) is random error (individual variation, measurement error, etc.)

The coefficients we estimate ARE the part-worth utilities. They tell us how much each unit change in an attribute affects the rating.
Important note about coding variables
In conjoint analysis, we can code attributes in different ways depending on their nature:

Continuous variables (e.g., premium in dollars, deductible in dollars): Treated as numeric values. The coefficient tells us the utility change per unit (e.g., per dollar).
Categorical variables (e.g., network size): Coded as dummy variables (0 or 1). The coefficient represents the utility difference between categories (e.g., Large network vs. Small network).

In our insurance example, Premium and Deductible are continuous (dollar amounts), while Network Size is categorical (Large vs. Small).


1.3 Generating the Experimental Design
First, we create all possible combinations of our attribute levels. With 3 attributes × 2 levels each, we have \(2^3 = 8\) possible profiles. This is called a full factorial design.

Now we use linear regression to estimate the part-worth utilities. We convert Network to a factor with “Small” as the reference level, so that the coefficient represents the utility gain from having a large network (vs. small):

# Convert network to a factor (Small = reference level)
rating_insurance <- rating_insurance %>%
  mutate(network = factor(network, levels = c("Small", "Large")))

# Fit linear regression model

                       data = rating_insurance)

summary(model_rating_ins)

Interpreting the coefficients (Part-Worth Utilities):

Intercept (8.51): The predicted rating when premium = $0, deductible = $0, and network = Small (the reference level). Since no real plan has a $0 premium and $0 deductible, this value is an extrapolation far outside our data range and should not be interpreted substantively. Deductible (-0.0008): Each $1,000 increase in annual deductible decreases rating by about 0.80 points.
networkLarge (0.55): Having a large network (vs. small) increases rating by about 0.55 points.

The regression coefficients (excluding the intercept) ARE the part-worth utilities. They directly tell us how much each attribute contributes to the overall rating.


1.6 Calculating Attribute Importance
Attribute importance tells us which features have the biggest impact on preferences. The calculation:

For each attribute, calculate the utility range: difference between highest and lowest part-worth values
Sum all the ranges
Express each range as a percentage of the total

Why does a larger range mean more important?
An attribute’s range tells us how much it can change someone’s overall evaluation. If premium has a utility range of 5 points and network has a range of 2 points, switching from worst to best premium gives you 5 utility points, while switching network levels only gives 2 points. The attribute with the larger range has more power to influence preferences.
CRITICAL CAVEAT: These importance scores are completely dependent on the range of levels you test. Testing premium of $200 vs. $201 would make premium appear unimportant, while $200 vs. $500 would make it appear very important. Importance scores do NOT tell us which attributes are “objectively most important.” They tell us which attributes have the most impact GIVEN THE SPECIFIC LEVELS YOU TESTED. Always choose attribute levels that reflect realistic market variation.
Let’s get regression coefficients and calculate importance:


Code
# 1. Extract coefficients
coef_ins <- coef(model_rating_ins)

# 2. Calculate utility at each level and the range
importance_rating_ins <- data.frame(
  attribute = c("Monthly Premium", "Annual Deductible", "Network Size"),
  highest_utility = c(
    coef_ins["premium"] * 200,       # Lowest premium ($200) = highest utility
    coef_ins["deductible"] * 500,     # Lowest deductible ($500) = highest utility
    coef_ins["networkLarge"] * 1      # Large network = highest utility
  ),
  lowest_utility = c(
    coef_ins["premium"] * 300,        # Highest premium ($300) = lowest utility
    coef_ins["deductible"] * 1500,    # Highest deductible ($1500) = lowest utility
    0                                  # Small network (reference) = 0
  )
)

importance_rating_ins <- importance_rating_ins %>%
  mutate(
    utility_range = abs(highest_utility - lowest_utility),
    importance_pct = utility_range / sum(utility_range) * 100
  )

1.7 Calculating Willingness-to-Pay (WTP)
Willingness-to-pay converts abstract utility values into concrete dollar amounts. This is possible because we included a price attribute (monthly premium) in our study.
The Logic:
If we know (1) how much utility a person gets from each attribute and (2) how much utility they lose per dollar of cost, we can calculate the dollar amount that would exactly offset any utility gain.
For example, if the utility of a large network is +0.6 points, and the utility loss per dollar of premium is -0.012 points, then: 0.6 / 0.012 = $50. This means respondents value a large network as much as they would value a $50 reduction in monthly premium.
The Formula: \[\text{WTP} = -\frac{\beta_{\text{attribute}}}{\beta_{\text{price}}}\]
WTP Calculations:
From our regression model:

Premium coefficient: -0.0116 utility points per dollar
Network coefficient: 0.5525 utility points for large network
Deductible coefficient: -0.0008 utility points per dollar

WTP for Large Network (vs. Small Network):
\[\text{WTP}_{\text{network}} = -\frac{0.5525}{-0.0116} = \$47.59\]
Interpretation: Respondents would be willing to pay an additional $47.59 per month to have access to a large provider network instead of a small network.
WTP for $1,000 Lower Deductible:
Applying the same logic, but scaling the deductible coefficient to a $1,000 change:
\[\text{WTP}_{\text{deductible}} = -\frac{\beta_{\text{deductible}} \times (-1000)}{\beta_{\text{premium}}} = -\frac{0.7725}{-0.0116} = \$66.54\]
Interpretation: Respondents would be willing to pay an additional $66.54 per month to reduce their annual deductible by $1,000.
Summary of WTP Estimates:



Attribute
WTP per Month




Large Network (vs. Small)
$47.59


$1,000 Lower Deductible
$66.54



Managerial Application:
These WTP values help managers make cost-benefit decisions:

Network expansion decision: If expanding the provider network costs the insurer $30 per member per month, and members are willing to pay $47.59 for it, the expansion is financially viable: the insurer can charge an additional $47.59 in premium while only incurring $30 in costs, creating a $17.59 per member margin.
Premium pricing for deductible tiers: Members are willing to pay $66.54 per month (or $798 annually) to reduce their deductible by $1,000. Offering a $1,000 lower deductible means insurance kicks in sooner, costing the insurer approximately $400 per year in additional claims. Since members would pay ~$798/year in extra premium for this benefit, the insurer captures a margin of approximately $398 per member per year.



1.8 Market Share Simulation
One of the most powerful applications of conjoint analysis is predicting how the market would respond to different product configurations.
The Process for Rating-Based Conjoint:

Define two (or more) competing options
Calculate the predicted rating for each option using the regression model
Convert ratings to market shares using proportional allocation

Proportional Allocation: If Plan A receives a predicted rating of 8 and Plan B receives 6, we allocate market share proportionally:
\[\text{Share}_A = \frac{8}{8+6} = 57\% \qquad \text{Share}_B = \frac{6}{8+6} = 43\%\]
Example Scenario:
Let’s compare two common plan designs:

Plan A (Premium Plan): $250/month premium, $500 annual deductible, Large network
Plan B (Budget Plan): $200/month premium, $1,500 annual deductible, Small network

Neither plan dominates the other: Plan A is better on deductible and network, while Plan B is better on premium.
Step 1: Calculate predicted ratings
Using the regression equation \(\text{Rating} = \beta_0 + \beta_1(\text{Premium}) + \beta_2(\text{Deductible}) + \beta_3(\text{Network})\):
Plan A (Premium Plan: $250, $500 deductible, Large network):
\[\text{Rating}_A = 8.51 + (-0.0116 \times 250) + (-0.0008 \times 500) + (0.55 \times 1) = 5.78\]
Plan B (Budget Plan: $200, $1,500 deductible, Small network):
\[\text{Rating}_B = 8.51 + (-0.0116 \times 200) + (-0.0008 \times 1500) + (0.55 \times 0) = 5.03\]
Step 2: Convert to market shares using proportional allocation
\[\text{Share}_A = \frac{5.78}{5.78 + 5.03} = 53.4\% \qquad \text{Share}_B = \frac{5.03}{5.78 + 5.03} = 46.6\%\]

Note on Method: Proportional allocation is a simple and intuitive approach, but it lacks theoretical grounding. It assumes that if Plan A gets a rating of 8 and Plan B gets a rating of 6, then exactly 57% of people will choose Plan A (8 ÷ 14 = 0.57). However, in reality, people make discrete yes/no choices, not proportional splits—someone either picks Plan A or they don’t. The method assumes market shares directly mirror rating differences, which oversimplifies how people actually choose. For important strategic decisions, choice-based methods with multinomial logit formulas (shown later) are theoretically more sound and preferred in practice because they model the actual choice process.

3.1 Conceptual Overview

Instead of rating profiles individually, respondents are shown choice sets containing two or more options and asked to pick their preferred one:

Which plan would you choose? ☐ Plan A ☐ Plan B

By forcing a choice, we ensure that respondents make explicit trade-offs. Someone who wants both low premium AND low deductible must decide which matters more.


3.2 Multinomial Logit Model
Choice-based conjoint uses multinomial logistic regression to analyze choice data. This method can handle choice sets with any number of alternatives (2, 3, 4, or more). We’ll use the mlogit package in R, which is the standard tool for discrete choice analysis.
Key Concept:
The model assumes people choose the alternative with the highest total utility. Each alternative’s total utility has two components:
\[U_i = V_i + \varepsilon_i\]

\(V_i = \beta_1 X_{i1} + \beta_2 X_{i2} + ... + \beta_k X_{ik}\) is the systematic (predictable) component, based on observed attributes
\(\varepsilon_i\) is the random component, representing individual taste variation and unmeasured factors

The logit formula converts the systematic utilities into choice probabilities (the random component is integrated out through the derivation):
\[P(\text{Choose alternative } i) = \frac{e^{V_i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{J} e^{V_j}}\]
where:

\(J\) is the total number of alternatives in the choice set
The coefficients (\(\beta_1, \beta_2, ..., \beta_k\)) are the part-worth utilities

Intuition: Alternatives with higher utility have exponentially higher choice probabilities. The model estimates the part-worth utilities (\(\beta\) coefficients) that best explain the observed choices.


3.3 Choice Data Format
The mlogit package requires data in long format — each row represents one alternative within a choice set, not one choice set per row. Note that the choice_set identifier must be unique across all respondents. That’s why we use IDs like 1_1, 1_2, … (meaning “respondent 1, choice set 1”, “respondent 1, choice set 2”, etc.) rather than simple numbers like 1, 2, 3. If two respondents both had a choice set labeled “1”, mlogit would incorrectly treat them as alternatives within the same choice set.
In other words, we need to clarify what each respondent saw and chose in each choice set.

The multinomial logit formula converts utilities into choice probabilities:

Then, calculate total range (sum all the ranges)
Finally, get each range as a percentage of the total

3.6 Willingness-to-Pay (Choice-Based)
We apply the same WTP formula as in the rating-based analysis. Because both methods estimate part-worth utilities and include a price attribute, the conversion logic is identical:
\[\text{WTP} = -\frac{\beta_{\text{attribute}}}{\beta_{\text{price}}}\]

\[\text{WTP}_{\text{network}} = -\frac{0.8145}{-0.0137} = \$59.37\]

\[\text{WTP}_{\text{deductible}} = -\frac{\beta_{\text{deductible}} \times (-1000)}{\beta_{\text{premium}}} = -\frac{0.6395}{-0.0137} = \$46.61\]

Consistent WTP findings across methods strengthen managerial confidence in the results. When the two methods produce similar WTP estimates, managers can trust that the preference data is robust — the underlying preferences are stable regardless of how respondents express them.


3.7 Market Share Simulation (Choice-Based)
For choice-based conjoint, we use the multinomial logit formula to predict market shares:
\[P(\text{Choose alternative } j) = \frac{e^{U_j}}{\sum_{k=1}^{J} e^{U_k}}\]

Step 1: Calculate systematic utilities
Using \(V = \beta_{\text{premium}} \times \text{premium} + \beta_{\text{deductible}} \times \text{deductible} + \beta_{\text{network}} \times \text{network}\):
Plan A (Premium Plan: $250, $500 deductible, Large network):
\[V_A = (-0.0137 \times 250) + (-0.0006 \times 500) + (0.8145 \times 1) = -2.94\]
Plan B (Budget Plan: $200, $1,500 deductible, Small network):
\[V_B = (-0.0137 \times 200) + (-0.0006 \times 1500) + (0.8145 \times 0) = -3.7\]
Step 2: Convert to market shares using the multinomial logit formula
\[\text{Share}_A = \frac{e^{-2.94}}{e^{-2.94} + e^{-3.7}} = 68.3\% \qquad \text{Share}_B = \frac{e^{-3.7}}{e^{-2.94} + e^{-3.7}} = 31.7\%\]
Key Difference from Rating-Based: Instead of dividing ratings proportionally, the logit formula exponentiates the utilities before computing shares. This is theoretically grounded in how people make discrete choices, making it more appropriate for predicting actual market behavior.
Interpretation: Based on the choice model, the Premium Plan is predicted to capture approximately 68% of the market. This is consistent with the rating-based results, reinforcing that the low deductible and large network more than compensate for the higher premium. From a managerial perspective:

The Premium Plan captures approximately 68% of the market despite costing $50/month more, indicating that the low deductible and large network are valued enough to justify the higher price
The Budget Plan still captures approximately 32%, suggesting a price-sensitive segment exists that prioritizes lower premiums

title: Conjoint Analysis in Healthcare Management
text:
Key Takeaways

Part-worth utilities (regression coefficients) tell us how much each attribute level contributes to overall preference
Attribute importance is calculated from the range of utilities within each attribute — the wider the range, the more influence that attribute has on preferences
WTP converts utility into dollar values using the price coefficient as the exchange rate: \(\text{WTP} = -\beta_{\text{attribute}} / \beta_{\text{price}}\). This requires a price attribute in the study design
Market share simulation predicts how respondents would split across competing options — using proportional allocation (rating-based) or the logit formula (choice-based)
Data structure matters: Choice-based conjoint requires long-format data with proper indexing so that mlogit knows which alternatives belong to each choice set
The managerial insight: Conjoint analysis transforms subjective preferences into quantitative data that supports concrete decisions about pricing, feature prioritization, and competitive strategy

title: Logistic Regression: Predicting Binary Outcomes in Healthcare
text:
In healthcare management, many of the most critical decisions involve predicting binary outcomes. For example,

Will an event happen or not?
Will a patient be readmitted within 30 days or not?
Will a patient adhere to their medication regimen or not?
Will a treatment be successful or not?

These yes/no questions are fundamentally different from predicting continuous outcomes like blood pressure or length of stay.
Let’s think about the following scenario:
A hospital administrator wants to identify patients at high risk of readmission (returning to the hospital after being released) so that care coordinators can provide additional support before discharge. The outcome variable, readmission, can only take two values: YES (the patient was readmitted) or NO (the patient was not readmitted). We cannot use regular linear regression for this problem because linear regression is designed to predict continuous outcomes that can take any value.
Logistic regression is an appropriate statistical technique when your outcome variable is binary. It allows us to:

Predict the probability that an event will occur
Identify which factors increase or decrease the likelihood of the outcome
Quantify the strength of each predictor’s effect
Make data-driven decisions about resource allocation and interventions




You might wonder why we cannot just use linear regression to predict a binary outcome coded as 0 and 1. Let’s understand why this approach fails.
Imagine we want to predict whether a patient will be readmitted (coded as 1) or not (coded as 0) based on their length of hospital stay (in days). If we use linear regression, we might get an equation like:
\[P(\text{Readmission}) = -0.2 + 0.05 \times \text{Length of Stay}\]
This seems reasonable at first, but there’s a fundamental problem. What if a patient has a very long length of stay of 30 days?
\[P(\text{Readmission}) = -0.2 + 0.05 \times 30 = 1.3\]
We get a probability greater than 1! But probabilities must be between 0 and 1. Similarly, for patients with very short stays, we could get negative probabilities. This is nonsensical. You cannot have a 130% chance or a -5% chance of being readmitted.
Linear regression assumes a straight-line relationship that extends infinitely in both directions. But probabilities are bounded between 0 and 1. We need a different approach that respects these boundaries.



Logistic regression solves this problem by using a special S-shaped curve (called the logistic function) that naturally stays between 0 and 1. Instead of predicting the probability directly with a straight line, logistic regression:

Transforms the probability into something called log odds
Models the log odds as a linear function of the predictors
Transforms the result back to a probability

This transformation ensures that no matter what values your predictors take, the predicted probability will always be between 0 and 1. The relationship “flattens out” at the extremes, creating the characteristic S-shape.









As you can see in the graph above, the linear regression line (red) extends beyond the valid probability range, while the logistic regression curve (blue) smoothly transitions between 0 and 1, approaching but never crossing these boundaries.
Now that we understand why we need logistic regression and how it solves the boundary problem, let’s explore the mathematical foundations that make it work.

title: Logistic Regression: Predicting Binary Outcomes in Healthcare
text:
From Probability to Odds
You may already be familiar with probability. It’s the chance that something will happen, expressed as a number between 0 and 1 (or as a percentage between 0% and 100%). For example, if 30 out of 100 patients are readmitted, the probability of readmission is 0.30 or 30%.
Odds express the same information in a different way. Instead of comparing the number of events to the total, odds compare the number of events happening to the number of events not happening:
\[\text{Odds} = \frac{p}{1-p} = \frac{\text{Probability of event happening}}{\text{Probability of event not happening}}\]
Using our readmission example:

Probability of readmission = 0.30
Probability of NOT being readmitted = 0.70
Odds of readmission = 0.30 / 0.70 = 0.429

This means that for every patient who is readmitted, there are about 2.3 patients who are not readmitted (since 1/0.429 ≈ 2.3). Alternatively, we can say the odds are “0.429 to 1” or roughly “7 to 3” in favor of not being readmitted.

Understanding Odds Values
Here’s a helpful table showing how probability and odds relate to each other:

When odds = 1, the event is equally likely to happen or not happen (50/50 chance)

title: Logistic Regression: Predicting Binary Outcomes in Healthcare
text:
From Odds to Log Odds (Logit)
While odds are more useful than probabilities for our purposes (they range from 0 to infinity instead of 0 to 1), they still have a limitation: they cannot be negative. This asymmetry makes them difficult to model with linear equations.
The solution is to take the natural logarithm of the odds, which gives us the log odds (also called the logit):
\[\text{Log Odds} = \ln(\text{Odds}) = \ln\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)\]
This transformation has a beautiful property: log odds can range from negative infinity to positive infinity, making them perfect for linear modeling.

Log odds can be any real number (positive or negative)

The log odds transformation is what makes logistic regression work. It converts the bounded probability (0 to 1) into an unbounded scale that can be modeled with a linear equation.

title: Logistic Regression: Predicting Binary Outcomes in Healthcare
text:
The Logistic Regression Equation
Now we can write the logistic regression equation. Instead of predicting probability directly (which would cause the boundary problems we discussed), we predict the log odds:
\[\ln\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \cdots + \beta_k X_k\]
where p is the probability of the outcome (e.g., probability of readmission).
This equation indicates that “the log odds of the outcome is a linear combination of the predictors.”
The coefficients (\(\beta\) values) in this equation are log odds ratios, which tell us how much the log odds change when the predictor increases by one unit.
By using this equation, we can get predicted log odds.

Converting Back to Probability
Once we have predicted log odds, we can convert back to probability using these relationships:

From log odds to odds: \(\text{Odds} = e^{\text{log odds}}\) (exponentiated log odds)
From odds to probability: \(p = \frac{\text{Odds}}{1 + \text{Odds}}\)

Or in one step:
\[p = \frac{e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \cdots}}{1 + e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \cdots}}\]
Don’t worry if these formulas seem complex. R will do all these calculations for us (that’s why we use statistical software!). The important thing is to understand the conceptual flow: (1) we model log odds linearly, then (2) transform the results back to probabilities.

title: Logistic Regression: Predicting Binary Outcomes in Healthcare
text:
Estimation Method: Maximum Likelihood Estimation
Unlike linear regression, we cannot use the OLS method, because:

Probability must stay between 0 and 1: OLS could predict probabilities outside this range (e.g., -0.3 or 1.4), which doesn’t make sense.
Binary outcomes violate OLS assumptions: The residuals in binary outcomes can’t be normally distributed (as they can only take on two values).
Non-constant variance: When outcomes are binary, the variance changes systematically with the predicted probability, violating the OLS assumption of constant variance (homoscedasticity).

Logistic regression uses Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE), a different approach that:

Finds the coefficient values (parameters) that make the observed data most likely to have occurred
Naturally respects the probability boundaries (predictions always stay between 0 and 1)
Works well with the binomial distribution of binary outcomes

You don’t need to understand the mathematics of MLE for this course. The key point is that the estimation method is different from linear regression, but R handles all the computation automatically. When you use the glm() function with family = binomial, R is using MLE behind the scenes.

title: Logistic Regression in Healthcare Management
section: 4.1 Simple Logistic Regression Example: Predicting Hospital Readmission
text:
4.1 Simple Logistic Regression Example: Predicting Hospital Readmission
You are a quality improvement analyst at a regional hospital. Hospital readmissions within 30 days are a major concern because they indicate potential gaps in care quality and result in financial penalties under Medicare’s Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program.
Your hospital has been tracking patient satisfaction scores (measured on a 1-10 scale at discharge) and wants to understand: Does patient satisfaction predict the likelihood of 30-day readmission?
The hypothesis is that patients who are more satisfied with their care may be better prepared for discharge, have better understanding of their follow-up instructions, and therefore be less likely to be readmitted.
The Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program (HRRP), established by the Affordable Care Act in 2012, penalizes hospitals with excess readmissions for specific conditions. Research has shown that patient experience metrics, including satisfaction scores, are associated with readmission rates, though the relationship is complex and influenced by multiple factors including patient demographics, clinical complexity, and post-discharge support systems.

title: Logistic Regression in Healthcare Management
text:
4.2 Creating and Exploring the Data
Let’s first create our dataset and explore it to understand what we’re working with. Our dataset includes not only patient satisfaction but also other important factors like age, comorbidities, and insurance type. For this simple regression example, we’ll focus only on satisfaction, but having all these variables in the dataset will allow us to compare simple vs. multiple regression later.

# Create comprehensive readmission dataset
n <- 200

# Generate predictor variables
satisfaction <- round(runif(n, min = 3, max = 10), 1)
age <- round(rnorm(n, mean = 65, sd = 12))
age <- pmax(pmin(age, 95), 30)  # Keep age between 30 and 95
comorbidities <- rpois(n, lambda = 2)  # Number of chronic conditions
insurance <- sample(c("Private", "Medicare", "Medicaid"), n,
                    replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.4, 0.4, 0.2))

# Generate readmission outcomes based on all predictors
# Higher satisfaction = lower risk
# Higher age = higher risk
# More comorbidities = higher risk
# Insurance type affects risk
insurance_effect <- ifelse(insurance == "Private", -0.5,
                    ifelse(insurance == "Medicare", 0, 0.4))

log_odds <- -2 - 0.325 * satisfaction + 0.02 * age + 0.6 * comorbidities +
            insurance_effect + rnorm(n, 0, 0.5)
prob_readmit <- exp(log_odds) / (1 + exp(log_odds))
readmitted <- rbinom(n, 1, prob_readmit)

# Create data frame
readmit_data <- data.frame(
  patient_id = 1:n,
  satisfaction = satisfaction,
  age = age,
  comorbidities = comorbidities,
  insurance = factor(insurance),
  readmitted = readmitted
)

1.5 Running the Logistic Regression
In R, we use the glm() function (Generalized Linear Model) to run logistic regression. The key arguments are:

formula: Specifies the outcome and predictors (e.g., readmitted ~ discharge_readiness)
data: The dataset to use
family = binomial: Tells R to use logistic regression for binary outcomes

The syntax is similar to linear regression with lm(), but we add family = binomial(link = "logit") or just family = binomial (the default link function for binomial is logit):

# Fit logistic regression model
model_simple <- glm(readmitted ~ discharge_readiness,
                    data = readmit_data,
                    family = binomial(link = "logit"))

# View the results
summary(model_simple)

text:
1.6 Interpreting the Results Step by Step
The output contains a lot of information. Let’s work through it piece by piece to understand what it all means.

Step 1: Understanding the Coefficients Table
The most important part of the output is the “Coefficients” table. Let’s take a look at it:






Estimate
Std. Error
z value

(Intercept)

-0.1814

Each row in this table represents one term in our model:

(Intercept): This is \(\beta_0\), the predicted log odds when discharge readiness = 0
discharge_readiness: This is \(\beta_1\), the change in log odds for each one-unit increase in discharge readiness

The columns tell us:

Estimate: The coefficient value (log odds ratio)
Std. Error: The uncertainty in our estimate
z value: The test statistic (Estimate / Std. Error)
Pr(>|z|): The p-value for testing whether the coefficient significantly differs from zero



Step 2: Writing the Model Equation
From our output, we can write the logistic regression equation:
Log Odds of Readmission = -0.183 + (-0.1814) × Discharge Readiness
This equation tells us that, for each one-unit increase in discharge readiness score, the log odds of readmission changes by the coefficient value.


Step 3: Interpreting the Log Odds Ratio
The coefficient for discharge readiness is our log odds ratio. Let’s interpret it:
Log Odds Ratio for Discharge Readiness: -0.1814
Interpretation:

DIRECTION: The coefficient is NEGATIVE, which means higher discharge readiness is associated with LOWER log odds of readmission.
STATISTICAL SIGNIFICANCE: The p-value is 0.0401. Since p < 0.05, this relationship is statistically significant.
MAGNITUDE: For each one-unit increase in discharge readiness score, the log odds of readmission change by -0.1814.



Step 4: Converting to Odds Ratio
While log odds ratios are mathematically convenient, odds ratios are much easier to interpret. We convert by exponentiating:
\[\text{Odds Ratio} = e^{\text{Log Odds Ratio}}\]
We can get Odds Ratio by using the following R functions:

coef(): Extracts coefficients from the model
exp(): Exponentiates values (raises e to the power of the value) to convert log odds ratios to odds ratios


# Calculate odds ratios
odds_ratios <- exp(coef(model_simple))

Then, we get Odds Ratios:

Intercept: 0.8328
Discharge Readiness: 0.8341

Let’s interpret the odds ratio for discharge readiness:
Interpretation:

Since the odds ratio is LESS than 1, higher discharge readiness is associated with LOWER odds of readmission.
For each one-unit increase in discharge readiness score, the odds of readmission DECREASE by 16.6%. (or alternatively, the odds of readmission are multiplied by 0.834 for each one-unit increase in discharge readiness).

title: Logistic Regression: Predicting Binary Outcomes in Healthcare
text:
1.7 Predicting Probabilities
One of the most useful applications of logistic regression is predicting the probability of the outcome for specific values of the predictor. Let’s calculate predicted probabilities step by step.

1.7.1 Manual Calculation
Let’s predict the probability of readmission for a new patient with a discharge readiness score of 5:
Step 1: Calculate Predicted Log Odds
First, we use the logistic regression equation to calculate the log odds. We plug the discharge readiness score into our model equation with the estimated coefficients:
Log odds = -0.183 + (-0.181) × 5 = -1.0898
This log odds value represents the predicted log odds of readmission on the logit scale. To interpret this meaningfully, we need to convert it to odds and then to probability.
Step 2: Convert Log Odds to Odds
Next, we convert the log odds to odds by exponentiating (taking e to the power of the log odds):
\[\text{Odds} = e^{-1.0898} = 0.3363\]
This odds value tells us the ratio of the probability of readmission to the probability of not being readmitted. An odds value of 0.3363 means that readmission is less likely than not being readmitted.
Step 3: Convert Odds to Probability
Finally, we convert odds to probability using the formula: Probability = Odds / (1 + Odds)
\[\text{Probability} = \frac{0.3363}{1 + 0.3363} = 0.2517\]
A patient with a discharge readiness score of 5 has a 25.2% predicted probability of being readmitted within 30 days. This means that if we had 100 patients with this discharge readiness level, we would expect approximately 25 of them to be readmitted.


1.7.2 Using R’s predict() Function
While the manual calculation helps us understand the underlying process, in practice we use R’s predict() function to efficiently calculate predicted probabilities for many observations at once. This function automatically performs all three steps (log odds → odds → probability) for us.
The predict() function in R generates predictions from a fitted model. Key arguments are:

First argument: The fitted model object
newdata: A data frame containing the predictor values for which you want predictions
type = "response": Returns predicted probabilities (for logistic regression). Without this, it returns log odds.

Let’s predict readmission probabilities for patients with different discharge readiness levels:
Predicted Probabilities of Readmission:


Code
# Create data frame with values to predict (5 new patients)
new_patients <- data.frame(
  discharge_readiness = c(4, 5, 6, 7, 8)
)

new_patients$predicted_prob <- predict(model_simple,
                                        newdata = new_patients,
                                        type = "response")

kable(round(new_patients, 3),
      col.names = c("Discharge Readiness Score", "Predicted Probability"),
      align = c("c", "c")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = FALSE)





Discharge Readiness Score
Predicted Probability




4
0.287


5
0.252


6
0.219
