As discharge readiness scores increase from 4 to 8, the predicted probability of readmission systematically decreases. This quantifies the relationship we observed in our earlier boxplot: higher discharge readiness is associated with lower readmission risk. We can use these probabilities to identify which patients may need additional discharge support.


1.7.3 Visualizing the Predicted Probabilities
Visualizing the relationship between our predictor and the predicted probability helps us understand the model and communicate findings to stakeholders. Let’s create a graph showing how the predicted probability of readmission changes across the full range of discharge readiness scores:


Code
# Create prediction data across range of discharge readiness
pred_data <- data.frame(
  discharge_readiness = seq(3, 10, by = 0.1)
)
pred_data$probability <- predict(model_simple, newdata = pred_data, type = "response")

# Plot
ggplot() +
  # Add prediction curve
  geom_line(data = pred_data, aes(x = discharge_readiness, y = probability),
            color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.2) +
  # Add actual data points
  geom_point(data = readmit_data, aes(x = discharge_readiness, y = readmitted),
             alpha = 0.3, position = position_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0)) +
  # Add reference line at 0.5
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  labs(title = "Predicted Probability of Readmission by Discharge Readiness Score",
       subtitle = "Points show actual patient outcomes (0 = not readmitted, 1 = readmitted)",
       x = "Discharge Readiness Score",
       y = "Predicted Probability of Readmission") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::percent) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))









Understanding this visualization:
The blue curve represents our model’s predicted probabilities across all discharge readiness levels. The black points show the actual patient outcomes in our dataset.
Key features of the logistic curve:

At low discharge readiness scores (left side): The probability of readmission is relatively high.
At high discharge readiness scores (right side): The probability of readmission is relatively low.

The dashed line at 0.5 (50%) represents the traditional classification threshold used in many statistical applications. However, in practice, we would likely use a much lower threshold for readmission prediction (e.g., 10-20%). Why? Because:

Actual readmission rates are typically around 15%, not 50%
The cost of missing a high-risk patient (false negative) is high
The cost of providing extra discharge support to a lower-risk patient (false positive) is relatively low

For example, if we used a 15% threshold, any patient with predicted probability ≥ 15 % would receive enhanced discharge planning. This more conservative approach helps ensure we don’t miss high-risk patients who could benefit from intervention.

title: Logistic Regression: Predicting Binary Outcomes in Healthcare
text:
1.8 Evaluating Model Performance
After fitting a logistic regression model, we want to assess its practical usefulness. In other words: How well does this model actually predict outcomes? While our model provides probabilities, in many healthcare applications we need to make binary decisions (e.g., “provide extra discharge support” vs. “standard discharge”). This requires evaluating how accurately our model classifies patients.

1.8.1 Creating a Classification Table
To evaluate classification performance, we first convert predicted probabilities into predicted classes using a decision threshold.
For this example, we’ll use the traditional 0.5 (50%) threshold to demonstrate how classification tables work:

If predicted probability ≥ 0.5 → predict “readmitted” (class = 1)
If predicted probability < 0.5 → predict “not readmitted” (class = 0)

While 0.5 is the standard default, in practice a lower threshold (e.g., 0.15-0.20) may be more appropriate for readmission prediction, since readmission rates are typically well below 50%.
We then create a classification table (also called a confusion matrix) that compares our predictions to actual outcomes:
Classification Table (Confusion Matrix):












Actual Outcome



Predicted Outcome
0
1




0
156
44


1
0
0







1.8.2 Interpreting the Classification Table
This 2×2 table shows four possible outcomes:

True Negatives (TN, top-left): Patients we correctly predicted would NOT be readmitted
False Negatives (FN, top-right): Patients we incorrectly predicted would NOT be readmitted (missed case)
False Positives (FP, bottom-left): Patients we incorrectly predicted would be readmitted (false alarm)
True Positives (TP, bottom-right): Patients we correctly predicted would be readmitted



1.8.3 Calculating Model Accuracy
Accuracy measures the overall proportion of correct predictions (both true positives and true negatives) out of all predictions:
\[\text{Accuracy} = \frac{\text{True Positives} + \text{True Negatives}}{\text{Total Number of Observations}} = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN}\]
Let’s calculate our model’s accuracy:
Model Performance:

Correctly classified: 156 out of 200 patients
Overall accuracy: 78%

Breakdown:

Correctly predicted NOT readmitted (True Negatives): 156
Correctly predicted readmitted (True Positives): 0
Incorrectly predicted readmitted (False Positives - false alarm): 0
Incorrectly predicted NOT readmitted (False Negatives - missed): 44

What does this mean?
Our model correctly classified 78% of patients. While accuracy is a useful starting point, in healthcare applications we often care more about specific types of errors. For example:

False negatives (missed readmissions) mean high-risk patients don’t receive intervention
False positives (false alarms) mean resources are spent on patients who don’t need extra support

The relative importance of these errors depends on the costs and benefits of intervention in your specific context.

title: Logistic Regression in Healthcare Management
section: 5.1 Multiple Logistic Regression Example: Comprehensive Readmission Risk Model
text:
5.1 Multiple Logistic Regression Example: Comprehensive Readmission Risk Model
Continuing with our hospital readmission example, the quality improvement team wants to build a more comprehensive model. They believe that readmission risk depends not only on patient satisfaction (satisfaction) but also on:

Patient age (age): older patients may have more complex health needs
Number of comorbidities (comorbidities): patients with multiple chronic conditions may be at higher risk
Insurance type (insurance): which may reflect access to post-discharge care

Our goal is to understand how each of these factors contributes to readmission risk while accounting for the others.

title: Logistic Regression in Healthcare Management
text:
5.2 Revisiting Our Readmission Dataset
Let’s return to the readmit_data dataset we created at the beginning. In the simple regression section, we focused only on the relationship between satisfaction and readmission. However, our dataset actually includes several other important variables that we haven’t used yet:

Age: Patient age in years
Comorbidities: Number of chronic health conditions
Insurance type: Private, Medicare, or Medicaid

This is the beauty of planning ahead in data analysis! By including these variables from the start, we can now build a more comprehensive model to answer a critical question:
Does patient satisfaction still predict readmission when we account for age, health complexity, and insurance type?
This question gets at the heart of why we need multiple regression. What if the satisfaction effect we found in simple regression was partly due to confounding? For example, perhaps younger, healthier patients tend to have higher satisfaction scores AND are naturally less likely to be readmitted. Without controlling for age and comorbidities, we might be overstating the true effect of satisfaction.
Our dataset (readmit_data) contains 200 patients with the following variables:

patient_id: Unique identifier for each patient
satisfaction: Patient satisfaction score at discharge (1-10 scale)
age: Patient age in years
comorbidities: Number of chronic health conditions (e.g., diabetes, hypertension, heart disease)
insurance: Insurance type (Private, Medicare, or Medicaid)
readmitted: Whether the patient was readmitted within 30 days (1 = yes, 0 = no)

Notice that we have both continuous predictors (satisfaction, age, comorbidities) and a categorical predictor (insurance type). Multiple logistic regression can handle both types of predictors simultaneously.

2.4 Running Multiple Logistic Regression
We understand our data, so we’re ready to fit the multiple logistic regression model. The good news is that the syntax is very similar to simple logistic regression. We just add more predictors to the formula using the + sign.
Remember from simple regression, we had: readmitted ~ discharge_readiness
Now with multiple predictors, we expand this to: readmitted ~ discharge_readiness + age + comorbidities + insurance
Each predictor is added to the right side of the formula, separated by plus signs. Let’s fit the model:

# Fit multiple logistic regression model

title: Logistic Regression in Healthcare Management
section: 5.5 Comparing Simple vs. Multiple Regression: Why Controlling for Confounders Matters
text:
5.5 Comparing Simple vs. Multiple Regression: Why Controlling for Confounders Matters
As we’ve built both a simple logistic regression (with satisfaction only) and a multiple logistic regression (with satisfaction, age, comorbidities, and insurance), let’s compare them to understand why multiple regression is necessary.

5.5.1 The Satisfaction Coefficient: Simple vs. Multiple Regression
Comparison of Satisfaction Effect:





Model
Log Odds Ratio
Odds Ratio
% Change in Odds




Simple Regression
-0.1814
0.834
-16.6%


Multiple Regression
-0.2183
0.804
-19.6%





Notice that the absolute satisfaction coefficient is larger in the multiple regression compared to the simple regression.

In the simple regression, we found that each 1-point increase in satisfaction was associated with a 16.6% decrease in the odds of readmission.
In the multiple regression, after controlling for age, comorbidities, and insurance type, each 1-point increase in satisfaction is associated with a 19.6% decrease in the odds of readmission.



5.5.2 Why Did the Coefficient Change?
This change reveals the presence of confounding. A confounder is a variable that is related to both the predictor we’re interested in (satisfaction) and the outcome (readmission), potentially creating a misleading relationship.
In our case, it’s possible that:

Younger, healthier patients (fewer comorbidities) tend to have higher satisfaction scores
Younger, healthier patients are also naturally less likely to be readmitted (regardless of their satisfaction)

Without controlling for age and comorbidities, the simple regression may have understated the true effect of satisfaction on readmission. The multiple regression gives us the “unique” effect of satisfaction by holding these other factors constant, essentially asking: “For two patients of the same age, with the same number of comorbidities, and the same insurance type, how does a difference in satisfaction affect readmission risk?”
This is why multiple regression is essential in healthcare analytics: it helps us isolate the independent effect of each factor and makes our conclusions more informative for decision-making.

title: Logistic Regression: Predicting Binary Outcomes in Healthcare
text:
2.6 Making Predictions with Multiple Predictors
With multiple logistic regression, we can make more nuanced predictions by considering a patient’s complete risk profile, not just one. Instead of just knowing their discharge readiness score, we now incorporate their age, health complexity, and insurance status to get a more accurate prediction.

2.6.1 Manual Calculation for Multiple Predictors
To understand how multiple predictors combine, let’s walk through a manual calculation for a specific patient. This shows the mathematical process, though in practice R will do this for us automatically.
The multiple logistic regression equation extends the simple version by adding more terms:
\[\text{Log Odds} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{Discharge Readiness} + \beta_2 \times \text{Age} + \beta_3 \times \text{Comorbidities}\] \[+ \beta_4 \times \text{Medicare} + \beta_5 \times \text{Private}\]
Example Patient:
Let’s assume that we have a new patient whose data is as follows, and we would like to predict this patient’s predicted probability of readmission using our multiple logistic regression model.

Discharge Readiness = 6
Age = 70
Comorbidities = 3
Insurance = Medicare

Step 1: Calculate Log Odds
Using the multiple logistic regression equation, we plug in all predictor values:
Log odds = -2.183 + (-0.218) × 6 + (0.0343) × 70 + (0.407) × 3 + (-1.188) × 1 + (-1.714) × 0
Log odds = -1.0564
Note: For Medicare insurance, we use 1 for the Medicare dummy variable and 0 for the Private dummy variable (since the patient doesn’t have private insurance).
Step 2: Convert to Odds
We can get the predicted odds by taking the exponent of the log odds.
\[\text{Odds} = e^{-1.0564} = 0.3477\]
Step 3: Convert to Probability
We can get the predicted probability by using the equation we learned above.
\[\text{Probability} = \frac{0.3477}{1 + 0.3477} = 0.258\]
This patient has a 25.8% predicted probability of readmission within 30 days.


2.6.2 Predictions for Multiple Patient Profiles
While manual calculations help us understand the mechanics, in practice we use R to generate predictions efficiently. One powerful use of multiple regression is creating risk profiles: comparing predicted probabilities for patients with different combinations of risk factors.
For example, we can contrast a “Low Risk” patient (young, few comorbidities, high discharge readiness, private insurance) with a “High Risk” patient (older, many comorbidities, low discharge readiness, Medicaid). Let’s create three representative profiles and see how their predicted probabilities differ:

# Create patient profiles
patient_profiles <- data.frame(
  discharge_readiness = c(8, 6, 4),
  age = c(50, 65, 80),
  comorbidities = c(1, 2, 4),
  insurance = factor(c("Private", "Medicare", "Medicaid"))
)

# Predict probabilities
patient_profiles$predicted_prob <- predict(model_multiple,
                                           newdata = patient_profiles,
                                           type = "response")

title: Logistic Regression in Healthcare Management
section: 6.1 The 0.5 Default Is Not Always Optimal
text:
6.1 The 0.5 Default Is Not Always Optimal
So far, we’ve used 0.5 as the probability cutoff for classification:

If predicted probability ≥ 0.5 → predict “event will occur” (e.g., readmitted)
If predicted probability < 0.5 → predict “event will not occur” (e.g., not readmitted)

But 0.5 is arbitrary. As we noted earlier when discussing readmission prediction, the optimal cutoff depends on your specific application. For hospital readmission, we mentioned that a lower threshold (e.g., 0.10-0.20) might be more appropriate because:

Actual readmission rates are typically 10-20%, not 50%
Missing a high-risk patient is costly
Providing extra support to lower-risk patients is relatively inexpensive

Let’s explore this more systematically by examining how different thresholds affect our predictions.

title: Logistic Regression in Healthcare Management
text:
6.2 Understanding the Trade-Off
When we change the cutoff threshold, we face a fundamental trade-off:
Lower threshold (e.g., 0.3):

We predict “event” more often
Catches more true positives (higher sensitivity)
But also more false alarms (lower specificity)

Higher threshold (e.g., 0.7):

We predict “event” less often
Fewer false alarms (higher specificity)
But misses more true positives (lower sensitivity)

title: Logistic Regression in Healthcare Management
text:
6.3 Sensitivity and Specificity
To understand how threshold choice affects our predictions, we need to introduce two critical metrics that measure different aspects of model performance. These metrics help us quantify the trade-offs we make when choosing a threshold.

6.3.1 Defining Sensitivity and Specificity
SENSITIVITY (True Positive Rate):
Of patients who were ACTUALLY readmitted, what percentage did we correctly identify?
\[\text{Sensitivity} = \frac{\text{True Positives}}{\text{True Positives} + \text{False Negatives}}\]
In other words, sensitivity measures the model’s ability to catch positive cases. (i.e., when a patient is readmitted, how often do we predict that they will be readmitted?) High sensitivity means we’re good at identifying patients who will be readmitted.
SPECIFICITY (True Negative Rate):
Of patients who were NOT readmitted, what percentage did we correctly identify?
\[\text{Specificity} = \frac{\text{True Negatives}}{\text{True Negatives} + \text{False Positives}}\]
In other words, specificity measures the model’s ability to correctly identify negative cases. (i.e., when a patient is not readmitted, how often do we predict that they will not be readmitted?) High specificity means we’re good at identifying patients who will not be readmitted.


6.3.2 The Inverse Relationship Between Sensitivity and Specificity
Here’s the crucial insight: sensitivity and specificity have an inverse relationship. When we adjust our threshold:

Lowering the threshold → We predict “positive” more often → More true positives captured (↑ sensitivity) BUT also more false positives (↓ specificity)
Raising the threshold → We predict “positive” less often → Fewer false positives (↑ specificity) BUT we miss more true positives (↓ sensitivity)

You cannot maximize both simultaneously. This creates a fundamental trade-off that requires us to think carefully about the costs and benefits of different types of errors in our specific application.
Think of it this way:

If you want to catch 100% of readmissions (perfect sensitivity), you’d need to flag almost everyone as high-risk, creating many false alarms (poor specificity).
If you want zero false alarms (perfect specificity), you’d flag almost no one, missing many actual readmissions (poor sensitivity).

The optimal threshold depends on which type of error is more costly in your context.


6.3.3 Calculating Sensitivity and Specificity for Our Model
Let’s calculate these metrics for our multiple regression model with the 0.5 cutoff:
With 0.5 cutoff:

Sensitivity: 18.2%

We correctly identified 18.2% of actual readmissions
Calculation: \(\frac{8}{8 + 36} = 0.182\)

Specificity: 98.1%

We correctly identified 98.1% of patients who were not readmitted
Calculation: \(\frac{153}{153 + 3} = 0.981\)


These values serve as our baseline. Now let’s see how they change when we adjust the threshold.

title: Logistic Regression in Healthcare Management
text:
6.4 Choosing the Right Threshold
The 0.5 cutoff is a default, but not necessarily optimal. Different thresholds create different trade-offs between sensitivity and specificity. Let’s compare three different cutoffs using our multiple regression model:

As you can see, as the threshold increases:

Sensitivity decreases (we miss more actual readmissions)
Specificity increases (we have fewer false alarms)

How to choose the optimal threshold?
The optimal threshold depends on your specific context and your interest:

Prioritize sensitivity (lower threshold): When missing a positive case is very costly (e.g., screening programs, low-cost interventions)
Prioritize specificity (higher threshold): When false alarms are costly due to limited resources or expensive interventions
Use default 0.5: When both types of errors have roughly equal costs

In healthcare practice, work with clinical stakeholders to understand the costs of different errors and choose a threshold that aligns with your organizational goals and resource constraints.

title: Logistic Regression in Healthcare Management
text:
7.1 When to Use Logistic Regression
Use logistic regression when:

Your outcome variable is binary (two possible values)
You want to predict the probability of an event occurring
You want to understand which factors increase or decrease the likelihood of the outcome
You need to quantify effects using odds ratios

title: Logistic Regression in Healthcare Management
text:
7.2 Interpreting Results

7.2.1 Log Odds Ratios (Coefficients)



Value
Meaning




= 0
No effect on log odds


< 0
Negative effect (decreases log odds)


> 0
Positive effect (increases log odds)



The further from 0, the stronger the effect.


7.2.2 Odds Ratios (Exponentiated Coefficients)



Value
Meaning




= 1
No effect on odds


< 1
Decreases odds (protective factor)


> 1
Increases odds (risk factor)



The further from 1, the stronger the effect.


7.2.3 Converting Between Measures
Probability → Odds → Log Odds
\[\text{Odds} = \frac{p}{1-p}\]
\[\text{Log Odds} = \ln(\text{Odds})\]
Log Odds → Odds → Probability
\[\text{Odds} = e^{\text{Log Odds}}\]
\[\text{Probability} = \frac{\text{Odds}}{1 + \text{Odds}}\]

title: Lab Assignment 3: ANOVA
text:
Step 1: Compute summary statistics.

los_data %>%
  group_by(department) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean = round(mean(los), 2),
    sd = round(sd(los), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

Step 2: Run a one-way ANOVA.

# One-way ANOVA
los_anova <- aov(los ~ department, data = los_data)
summary(los_anova)

Step 3: Run post-hoc comparisons using emmeans.

# Post-hoc pairwise comparisons
emm_los <- emmeans(los_anova, ~ department)
pairs(emm_los, adjust = "tukey")

Step 4: Create a box plot comparing LOS across departments.

ggplot(los_data, aes(x = department, y = los, fill = department)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Length of Stay by Department",
       x = "Department",
       y = "Length of Stay (days)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

Interpretation Questions:

Is the overall ANOVA significant? What does this tell you?
Which departments differ significantly from each other according to the post-hoc test? What operational recommendations would you make?







NoteAnswer Key




Yes, the overall ANOVA is significant (F(3, 76) = 22.02, p < 0.001), indicating that average length of stay differs significantly across the four departments (at least one department’s length of stay is significantly different from the others’).
The Emergency department (M = 2.81 days) has a significantly shorter LOS than Cardiology (M = 5.17), Orthopedics (M = 5.23), and Neurology (M = 4.49). However, there was no significant difference across Cardiology, Orthopedics, and Neurology departments. The manager should investigate whether the longer stays in Cardiology, Orthopedics, and Neurology imply clinical necessity (department specific characteristics) or potential inefficiencies in discharge processes.







Step 1: Compute summary statistics by time point.

recovery_data %>%
  group_by(time) %>%
  summarise(
    mean = round(mean(mobility), 1),
    sd = round(sd(mobility), 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

Step 2: Run a repeated-measures ANOVA. Remember: the same patients are measured at all time points, so use Error().

# Repeated-measures ANOVA
recovery_anova <- aov(mobility ~ time + Error(patient_id/time), data = recovery_data)
summary(recovery_anova)

Step 3: Run post-hoc comparisons.

emm_recovery <- emmeans(recovery_anova, ~ time)
pairs(emm_recovery, adjust = "tukey")

Interpretation Questions:

Is the effect of time significant? What does this mean for patient recovery?
Based on the post-hoc results, between which time points do we see the most significant improvement? Does recovery appear to plateau at any point?







NoteAnswer Key




Yes, the effect of time is significant (F(3, 72) = 430.9, p < 0.001), indicating that functional mobility scores change significantly across the recovery period (the mean mobility score at at least one time point is significantly different from those at the other time points).
The largest improvement occurs between Week 1 and Week 4 (increase of about 21 points), followed by Week 4 to Week 8 (increase of about 12 points), and Week 8 to Week 12 (increase of about 7 points). All pairwise comparisons are significant (p < 0.001), but the diminishing gains suggest recovery begins to plateau around Week 8-12.







Step 1: Create an interaction plot.

training_summary <- training_data %>%
    group_by(method, experience) %>%
    summarise(mean = mean(score), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(training_summary, aes(x = experience, y = mean, color = method, group = method)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  labs(title = "Competency by Training Method and Experience",
       x = "Experience Level",
       y = "Mean Competency Score",
       color = "Method") +
  theme_minimal()

Step 2: Run two-way between-subjects ANOVA.

training_anova <- aov(score ~ method * experience, data = training_data)
summary(training_anova)

Step 3: Run simple effects analysis.

emm_train <- emmeans(training_anova, ~ method | experience)
pairs(emm_train, adjust = "tukey")

Interpretation Questions:

Is the interaction significant? What does the interaction plot suggest about the pattern (parallel, ordinal, or disordinal)?
At which experience levels does the training method make a significant difference? What training strategy would you recommend?







NoteAnswer Key




Yes, the interaction is significant (F(2, 66) = 69.57, p < 0.001). The interaction plot shows a disordinal (crossover) pattern, which means that the effect of training method significantly differs depending on nurses’ experience levels.
Simple effects analysis shows that for Novice nurses, simulation method was significantly better than lecture method (Simulation is about 14 points higher), while for Expert nurses, lecture was significantly better than simulation (Lecture is about 10 points higher). However, for Intermediate nurses, there was no significant difference between the two methods. The recommendation would be to use simulation-based training for novice nurses and traditional lectures for expert nurses, while either method works equally well for intermediate-level nurses.







Step 1: Create an interaction plot.

comprehension_summary <- comprehension_data %>%
  group_by(mode, complexity) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(comprehension), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(comprehension_summary, aes(x = complexity, y = mean, color = mode, group = mode)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  labs(title = "Comprehension by Mode and Complexity",
       x = "Instruction Complexity",
       y = "Mean Comprehension Score",
       color = "Mode") +
  theme_minimal()

Step 2: Run two-way within-subjects ANOVA. Remember: both factors are within-subjects, so both go in Error().

comp_anova <- aov(comprehension ~ mode * complexity + Error(patient_id/(mode * complexity)),
                  data = comprehension_data)
summary(comp_anova)

Step 3: Run simple effects analysis.

emm_comp <- emmeans(comp_anova, ~ mode | complexity)
pairs(emm_comp, adjust = "tukey")

Interpretation Questions:

Is the interaction significant? What does this mean about how communication mode affects comprehension for simple vs. complex instructions?
For which instruction type does the communication mode matter more? What practical recommendation would you make for discharge planning?







NoteAnswer Key




Yes, the interaction is significant (F(1, 17) = 70.52, p < 0.001). This means that the effect of communication mode is significantly different depending on instruction complexity.
Communication mode matters for both instruction types, but the benefit is much larger for complex instructions (about 24 points gain) than for simple instructions (about 6 points gain). For discharge planning, clinics should provide written materials alongside verbal explanations for all discharge instructions, as it significantly improves comprehension in both cases. However, it is especially important to provide written materials for complex instructions, as the comprehension gain is substantially larger.







Step 1: Create an interaction plot.

diabetes_summary <- diabetes_data %>%
  group_by(group, time) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(hba1c), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(diabetes_summary, aes(x = time, y = mean, color = group, group = group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  labs(title = "HbA1c Trajectories by Education Program",
       x = "Time Point",
       y = "Mean HbA1c (%)",
       color = "Group") +
  theme_minimal()

Step 2: Run mixed design ANOVA. Remember: only the within-subjects factor (time) goes in Error().

diabetes_anova <- aov(hba1c ~ group * time + Error(patient_id/time),
                      data = diabetes_data)
summary(diabetes_anova)

Step 3: Run simple effects — compare groups at each time point.

emm_diabetes <- emmeans(diabetes_anova, ~ group | time)
pairs(emm_diabetes, adjust = "tukey")

Interpretation Questions:

Is the interaction significant? What does this tell you about the trajectories of the two groups?
At which time points do the groups differ significantly? If you were a clinic administrator, would you fund this program based on the 3-month results alone? Why or why not?







NoteAnswer Key




Yes, the interaction is significant (F(2, 96) = 52.1, p < 0.001), indicating that the HbA1c trajectories significantly differ between the two care groups over time.
Simple effects analysis showed that the groups do not differ significantly at Baseline, which confirms no initial preexisting difference between the two groups. They differ significantly at 3 Months and more strongly at 6 Months. The 3-month results alone already provide evidence of effectiveness to support funding the program. (However, the 6-month results reveal that the benefit gets significantly larger, suggesting that longer evaluation periods provide stronger evidence.)

title: Lab Assignment 2: t-tests (Week 05)
text:
One-sample t-test
Independent-samples t-test
Paired-samples t-test
One-sample t-test





Step 1: Extract the readmission data and compute descriptive statistics.

# Extract readmission days
readmission <- qi_data$readmission_days

# Descriptive statistics
cat("Sample size:", length(readmission), "\n")
cat("Sample mean:", round(mean(readmission), 2), "days\n")
cat("Sample SD:", round(sd(readmission), 2), "\n")
cat("Benchmark:", 30, "days\n")

Step 2: Perform the one-sample t-test and view the results.

# Perform one-sample t-test comparing readmission days to the benchmark
result_readmission <- t.test(readmission, mu = 30)
parameters(result_readmission)

Interpretation Question: Based on the p-value, is the hospital’s average readmission time significantly different from the 30-day benchmark? What does this suggest for the quality improvement team?






NoteAnswer Key



Yes, the hospital’s average readmission time is significantly different from the 30-day benchmark (t(39) = -3.49, p = 0.001). The hospital’s mean readmission time (26.61 days) is significantly shorter than the 30-day national benchmark, suggesting that patients are being readmitted sooner than expected. The quality improvement team should investigate why patients are returning earlier, as this could indicate issues with discharge planning, inadequate post-discharge follow-up, premature discharge, etc.






Step 1: Separate the cost data by department and compute descriptive statistics.

# Extract treatment costs for each department
cardiology_cost <- qi_data$cost_of_care[qi_data$department == "Cardiology"]
orthopedics_cost <- qi_data$cost_of_care[qi_data$department == "Orthopedics"]

# Descriptive statistics
cat("Cardiology:\n")
cat("  Mean: $", round(mean(cardiology_cost), 2), "\n")
cat("  SD: $", round(sd(cardiology_cost), 2), "\n")
cat("  n:", length(cardiology_cost), "\n\n")

cat("Orthopedics:\n")
cat("  Mean: $", round(mean(orthopedics_cost), 2), "\n")
cat("  SD: $", round(sd(orthopedics_cost), 2), "\n")
cat("  n:", length(orthopedics_cost), "\n\n")

cat("Difference: $", round(mean(cardiology_cost) - mean(orthopedics_cost), 2))

Step 2: Perform the independent-samples t-test.

# Perform independent-samples t-test
result_cost <- t.test(cardiology_cost, orthopedics_cost, var.equal = TRUE)
parameters(result_cost)

Interpretation Question: Is there a statistically significant difference in treatment costs between the two departments? What recommendation would you make to hospital leadership regarding budget allocation?






NoteAnswer Key



No. The treatment cost of Cardiology department (M = $14,098.35) was higher than that of Orthopedics (M = $13,576.65) department (t(38) = 0.66, p = 0.516), but the difference was not statistically significant. Hospital leadership does not need to allocate significantly different budgets based on per-patient treatment costs, as both departments have similar cost structures.

       mapping = aes(x = department,

The box plot shows that the two departments’ cost distributions largely overlap, with similar medians and interquartile ranges. These largely overlapping distributions are consistent with the non-significant t-test result from Task 3, confirming that there is no notable difference in treatment costs between Cardiology and Orthopedics departments.






Step 1: Extract the paired data and compute descriptive statistics.

# Extract anxiety scores
anxiety_pre <- qi_data$anxiety_before
anxiety_post <- qi_data$anxiety_after

# Descriptive statistics
cat("Before MBSR:\n")
cat("  Mean:", round(mean(anxiety_pre), 2), "\n")
cat("  SD:", round(sd(anxiety_pre), 2), "\n\n")

cat("After MBSR:\n")
cat("  Mean:", round(mean(anxiety_post), 2), "\n")
cat("  SD:", round(sd(anxiety_post), 2), "\n\n")

cat("Mean difference:", round(mean(anxiety_pre - anxiety_post), 2), "points\n")

Step 2: Perform the paired-samples t-test.

# Perform paired-samples t-test
result_anxiety <- t.test(anxiety_pre, anxiety_post, paired = TRUE)
parameters(result_anxiety)

Interpretation Question: Based on the p-value, did the MBSR program significantly reduce patient anxiety? Would you recommend continuing the program?






NoteAnswer Key



Yes, the MBSR program significantly reduced patient anxiety (t(39) = 10.35, p < 0.001). Based on the significant anxiety reduction result, the hospital should continue the MBSR program as an effective intervention for reducing patient anxiety.







# Create data frame for visualization
anxiety_viz <- data.frame(
  patient = rep(1:40, 2),
  time = factor(rep(c("Before", "After"), each = 40),
                levels = c("Before", "After")),
  score = c(anxiety_pre, anxiety_post)
)

# Create spaghetti plot
ggplot(anxiety_viz, aes(x = time, y = score, group = patient)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3, color = "gray30") +
  geom_point(aes(color = time), size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  stat_summary(aes(group = 1), fun = mean, geom = "line",
               linewidth = 2, color = "red") +
  stat_summary(aes(group = 1), fun = mean, geom = "point",
               size = 4, color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Patient Anxiety Scores Before and After MBSR Program",
       subtitle = "Red line shows mean change",
       x = "",
       y = "Anxiety Score (0-10)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

Interpretation Question: What does the red line (mean) tell you about the overall effect? Do all patients show the same pattern, or is there individual variability?






NoteAnswer Key



The red line shows a clear downward trend in mean anxiety from before to after the MBSR program, confirming the overall effectiveness of the program. However, the individual gray lines reveal substantial variability (i.e., the reduction is not the same across individuals; some patients show little change or even a slight increase).

section: 2.1 Crestview Medical Center Quality Improvement Study
text:
2.1 Crestview Medical Center Quality Improvement Study
Crestview Medical Center is a 250-bed community hospital that launched a system-wide quality improvement (QI) initiative to evaluate patient outcomes, operational efficiency, and care delivery models. The hospital collected data on 150 patients across four clinical departments over a 6-month period. Two care delivery models were compared: the existing Standard pathway and a newly piloted Coordinated pathway featuring multidisciplinary care teams.
As a healthcare analyst, you are asked to analyze this dataset to provide actionable insights to hospital leadership.

title: Midterm Exam: Healthcare Data Analytics
text:
2.2 Loading the Data
Run the code below to load required packages and the dataset.

# Load required packages
library(tidyverse)

title: Lab Assignment 4: Crosstabulation and Correlation
text:
Step 1: Create a contingency table and run a chi-square test.

# Create contingency table
discharge_table <- table(discharge_data$disposition, discharge_data$readmission)
discharge_table

# Run chi-square test
chi_discharge <- chisq.test(discharge_table)

# Check expected frequencies
chi_discharge$expected

# Display test results
chi_discharge

Step 2: Calculate row percentages to see readmission rates by disposition.

row_pct <- prop.table(discharge_table, margin = 1) * 100
row_pct

Step 3: Create a grouped bar chart of readmission rates by disposition.

plot_data <- as.data.frame(row_pct)
colnames(plot_data) <- c("disposition", "readmission", "percentage")

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = disposition, y = percentage, fill = readmission)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge", alpha = 0.8, width = 0.4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", percentage)),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.4),
            vjust = -0.5, size = 3.5) +
  labs(title = "Readmission Rates by Discharge Disposition",
       x = "Discharge Disposition",
       y = "Percentage of Patients") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

Interpretation Questions:

Are all expected frequencies ≥ 5? Is the chi-square test appropriate for this data?
Is the association between discharge disposition and readmission statistically significant? Report the χ² value, df, and p-value.
Which disposition type has the highest and lowest readmission rates? What does this suggest for care transition planning?







NoteAnswer Key




Yes, all expected frequencies are ≥ 5. The chi-square test is appropriate for this data.
Yes, the association between discharge disposition and 30-day readmission is statistically significant (χ² = 7.207, df = 2, p = 0.027). Since p < 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis of independence.
SNF (Skilled Nursing Facility) has the highest readmission rate (31.8%), while Rehabilitation Center has the lowest (12.5%). This suggests that SNF patients may need more intensive post-discharge follow-up or enhanced care transition support to reduce readmissions.







Step 1: Create a scatterplot with a trend line.

ggplot(finance_data, aes(x = length_of_stay, y = total_charges_k)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 3, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Length of Stay vs. Total Charges",
       x = "Length of Stay (days)",
       y = "Total Charges ($1,000s)") +
  theme_minimal()

Step 2: Run a Pearson correlation test.

with(finance_data, cor.test(length_of_stay, total_charges_k, method = "pearson"))

Interpretation Questions:

What is the Pearson correlation coefficient (r)? What is the direction of the association, and how would you classify its strength (very weak, weak, moderate, strong, very strong)?
Is the correlation statistically significant? Report the t-statistic and p-value.
What does this relationship suggest for hospital financial planning?







NoteAnswer Key




The Pearson correlation coefficient is r = 0.929, indicating a very strong positive correlation between length of stay and total charges.
Yes, the positive correlation is highly statistically significant (t = 22.18, p < 2.2e-16).
The strong positive correlation indicates that longer hospital stays are associated with substantially higher costs. For financial planning, hospitals can use LOS as a reliable predictor of patient charges for budgeting and resource allocation.







Step 1: Create a scatterplot (use jitter since acuity is discrete).

ggplot(ed_triage_data, aes(x = acuity_level, y = time_to_treatment_min)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 3,
             position = position_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "red") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:5) +
  labs(title = "Time to Treatment by Triage Acuity Level",
       x = "Triage Acuity Level (1 = Most Acute, 5 = Non-urgent)",
       y = "Time to Treatment (minutes)") +
  theme_minimal()

Step 2: Run a Spearman correlation test.

with(ed_triage_data, cor.test(acuity_level, time_to_treatment_min, method = "spearman"))

Interpretation Questions:

What is the Spearman correlation coefficient (ρ)? Is it positive or negative? Explain why the direction makes clinical sense.
Is the correlation statistically significant? Report the p-value.
Why is Spearman more appropriate than Pearson for this data? (Hint: think about the measurement scale of acuity)







NoteAnswer Key




The Spearman correlation coefficient is ρ = 0.863, which is a strong positive correlation. The positive direction makes clinical sense because higher acuity numbers indicate less urgent conditions (5 = Non-urgent), and these less urgent patients are less prioritized and wait longer for treatment.
Yes, the correlation is highly statistically significant (p < 2.2e-16).
Spearman correlation is more appropriate than Pearson because acuity is measured on an ordinal scale (ESI 1-5). The levels indicate rank order of severity, but the intervals between levels are not necessarily equal (e.g., the clinical difference between ESI 1 and 2 is not the same as between ESI 4 and 5). Spearman uses ranks rather than raw values, making it suitable for ordinal data.

title: Linear Regression 1: Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
In Week 8, we used correlation to answer whether there is a relationship between nurse staffing hours and patient satisfaction (e.g., r = 0.85).
Linear regression extends this by answering more detailed questions:

How many points does satisfaction increase for each additional nursing hour? (quantifying the relationship)
If we increase staffing to 8 hours per patient day, what satisfaction score can we expect? (making predictions)
Among wait time, staffing, and facility age, which factors significantly explain patient satisfaction? (identifying key drivers)
Does staffing still matter after controlling for facility age and patient severity? (controlling for confounding variables)

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Learning Goals
By the end of this lecture, you will be able to:

Understand when linear regression is used and how it works
Fit simple and multiple linear regression models in R using lm()
Interpret regression coefficients (direction, magnitude, significance)
Make predictions for new observations using fitted models
Identify multicollinearity using VIF and understand how to handle it

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
From Correlation to Regression
In Week 8, we used correlation to answer:

“Is there a relationship between nurse staffing hours and patient satisfaction?”


 Linear regression extends this by answering more actionable questions:

How many points does satisfaction change for each additional nursing hour?
If we increase staffing to 8 hours per patient day, what satisfaction score can we expect?
Among wait time, staffing, and facility age, which factors significantly explain patient satisfaction?

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Types of Linear Regression
Linear regression models the linear relationship between independent variables (IV) and a dependent variable (DV):

e.g., Are older patients more likely to have longer lengths of stay (LOS)?

Dependent variable (Y): The outcome we want to predict or explain (LOS)
Independent variable(s) (X): The predictor(s) we use to explain Y (age)



The number of independent variables determines the type of regression:

Simple Linear Regression: One predictor → outcome  (e.g., Patient age → LOS)
Multiple Linear Regression: Two or more predictors → outcome  (e.g., Age + Severity + Insurance → LOS)

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
What Is Simple Linear Regression?
Simple linear regression models the relationship between one independent variable (X) and one dependent variable (Y) using a straight line (linear model).


When to use it:

Quantify the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two continuous variables
Predict an outcome based on a single predictor
Test whether a linear relationship is statistically significant

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
The Model Equation
\[Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \epsilon_i\]


\(Y_i\) = Dependent variable: the outcome we predict (e.g., satisfaction score)
\(X_i\) = Independent variable: the predictor (e.g., wait time)
\(\beta_0\) = Intercept (a or b₀): predicted Y when X = 0 (The starting point)
\(\beta_1\) = Slope (b or b₁): change in Y per one-unit increase in X (“How much does Y change?”)
\(\epsilon_i\) = Residual: observed \(Y_i\) − predicted \(Y_i\) (\(\hat{Y}_i\))

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
The OLS Method
Linear regression finds the “best” line by minimizing the residual sum of squares (RSS):
\[RSS = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \epsilon_i^2\]


Let’s take a look at how the OLS method works in simple linear regression.

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Interpreting the Slope (β₁)
Now that we have the best-fit line, the slope (β₁) tells us:

Direction:

β₁ > 0: positive relationship
β₁ < 0: negative relationship

Magnitude: How much Y changes for each one-unit increase in X
Statistical significance: Whether the relationship likely exists in the population

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
section: Using the Fitted Model for Predictions
text:
Using the Fitted Model for Predictions
Once OLS estimates \(\beta_0\) (intercept) and \(\beta_1\) (slope), we can predict outcomes:
\[\hat{Y} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X\]


The “hat” notation (^) indicates estimated values from our sample data.


We use the fitted model to:

Assess model fit: predictions for observations in our dataset
Forecast outcomes: predictions for new observations
Evaluate “what if” questions: hypothetical scenarios

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
section: Example Case:  ED Wait Time & Patient Satisfaction
text:
Example Case:  ED Wait Time & Patient Satisfaction
Background: Research has consistently shown that ED wait times are negatively associated with patient satisfaction. A 2021 study (Abass et al.) found that being informed about waiting time showed a moderately strong positive correlation with patients’ overall rating.


Let’s build a regression model to quantify how much ED wait time impacts patient satisfaction scores, and use it to make predictions.

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Load the Data
Let’s load the required packages and dataset using the code:

library(tidyverse)

ed_data <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mba642-spring-26/mba642-spring-26.github.io/refs/heads/main/datasets/week11_ed_data.csv")

head(ed_data, 5) 

  X patient_id wait_time_minutes satisfaction_score
1 1          1                55               63.2
2 2          2                23               78.5
3 3          3                48               73.7
4 4          4                43               71.8
5 5          5                32               76.8

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Exploratory Data Analysis
Before running regression, always visualize your data:


Code
ggplot(ed_data, aes(x = wait_time_minutes, y = satisfaction_score)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 2, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "darkred", fill = "pink") +
  labs(
    x = "Wait Time (minutes)",
    y = "Patient Satisfaction Score (0-100)",
    title = "ED Wait Time vs. Patient Satisfaction"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()




Figure 1

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
section: Fitting the Simple Linear Regression Model
text:
Fitting the Simple Linear Regression Model
We use the lm(DV ~ IV, data) function in R:


Code
model_simple <- lm(satisfaction_score ~ wait_time_minutes, data = ed_data)
summary(model_simple)



Call:
lm(formula = satisfaction_score ~ wait_time_minutes, data = ed_data)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-21.2114  -5.0646  -0.5653   4.5972  16.9139 

Coefficients:
                  Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)       85.11385    1.39594   60.97   <2e-16 ***
wait_time_minutes -0.38228    0.02849  -13.42   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 7.01 on 148 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.5489,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.5458 
F-statistic: 180.1 on 1 and 148 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
The Fitted Regression Equation
Based on the model output, our fitted equation is:
\[\widehat{\text{Satisfaction}} = 85.11 + (-0.382) \times \text{Wait Time}\]

OLS found that when β₀ = 85.11 and β₁ = -0.382, the residual sum of squares (RSS) is minimized (i.e., this is the best-fitting line!)

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Interpreting the Results
1. The Intercept: β₀ = 85.11

When wait time is 0 minutes, predicted satisfaction is 85.11 points


2. The Slope: β₁ = -0.382

The effect of wait time on satisfaction score
Direction: Negative (longer waits -> lower satisfaction)
Magnitude: Each additional minute decreases satisfaction by 0.382 points
Significance: p = < 2.2e-16 (< 0.05) → statistically significant



3. R² = 0.549

Wait time explains 54.9% of the variance in satisfaction

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Visualizing R²


Figure 2

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Making Predictions: By Hand
Let’s predict satisfaction for a patient with a 45-minute wait:
Step 1: Recall the fitted equation
\[\widehat{\text{Satisfaction}} = 85.11 + (-0.382) \times \text{Wait Time}\]

Step 2: Plug in the value (X = 45)
\[\widehat{\text{Satisfaction}} = 85.11 + (-0.382) \times 45\]


Step 3: Calculate
\[\widehat{\text{Satisfaction}} = 67.91\]
The predicted satisfaction score for a patient with a 45-minute wait is 67.91 points.

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Making Predictions: In R
R makes this easier with the predict() function:

Let’s assume that we have 5 new patients and their wait times are 15, 30, 45, 60, and 90 minutes, respectively.


new_patients <- data.frame(
  wait_time_minutes = c(15, 30, 45, 60, 90)
)

new_patients$predicted_score <- predict(model_simple, newdata = new_patients)
new_patients

  wait_time_minutes predicted_score
1                15        79.37971
2                30        73.64557
3                45        67.91144
4                60        62.17730
5                90        50.70902

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
From Simple to Multiple Regression
Now that we’ve modeled the relationship between a single predictor and an outcome, a natural question arises:


What happens when multiple factors influence the outcome simultaneously?




In healthcare, outcomes are rarely driven by a single variable:

Patient satisfaction depends on more than just wait time
Length of stay depends on more than just age
Multiple linear regression addresses this reality

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
What Is Multiple Linear Regression?
Multiple linear regression extends simple regression to model the relationship between multiple independent variables and one dependent variable.


When to use it:

Include multiple predictors to better explain variance in an outcome
Control for confounding variables when examining specific relationships
Make predictions based on multiple characteristics simultaneously

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
The Model Equation
\[Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1i} + \beta_2 X_{2i} + \cdots + \beta_k X_{ki} + \epsilon_i\]


Example: Predicting patient satisfaction from care quality and wait time:
\[\widehat{\text{Satisfaction}} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{Care Quality} + \beta_2 \times \text{Wait Time}\]

β₁ is the effect of care quality on satisfaction (expected to be positive)
β₂ is the effect of wait time on satisfaction (expected to be negative)

text:
OLS in Multiple Linear Regression

OLS Simulation

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
section: Example Case: Hospital Length of Stay
text:
Example Case: Hospital Length of Stay
Background: A 2022 systematic review (Stone et al.) identified age, comorbidities, and severity as the most frequently cited predictors of hospital length of stay across 15 studies.


Let’s predict hospital LOS based on three key patient characteristics:

Age: Patient age in years
Severity Score: Illness severity on a 1-10 scale
Number of Comorbidities: Count of concurrent chronic conditions

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Load the Data
Let’s load the dataset using the code below:

hospital_data <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mba642-spring-26/mba642-spring-26.github.io/refs/heads/main/datasets/week11_hospital_data.csv")

head(hospital_data, 5)

  X patient_id age severity_score num_comorbidities length_of_stay
1 1          1  64            7.1                 2           11.9
2 2          2  75            5.6                 1            7.9
3 3          3  61            5.9                 1            8.3
4 4          4  56            1.6                 1            5.8
5 5          5  83            6.7                 1           10.8

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Fitting the Multiple Regression Model
Just like simple regression, we use the lm() function:


Code
model_multiple <- lm(length_of_stay ~ age + severity_score + num_comorbidities,
                     data = hospital_data)

summary(model_multiple)



Call:
lm(formula = length_of_stay ~ age + severity_score + num_comorbidities, 
    data = hospital_data)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-4.5147 -0.9968  0.0364  1.1500  3.6581 

Coefficients:
                  Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)       1.312040   0.376488   3.485 0.000567 ***
age               0.040739   0.005269   7.732 1.67e-13 ***
severity_score    0.623629   0.033959  18.364  < 2e-16 ***
num_comorbidities 0.793316   0.064185  12.360  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 1.556 on 296 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.6482,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.6446 
F-statistic: 181.8 on 3 and 296 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Interpreting the Coefficients
In multiple linear regression, each coefficient indicates the effect of the predictor holding all other variables constant:

Intercept (β₀ = 1.31): Predicted LOS when all predictors = 0 (not practically meaningful)
Age (β₁ = 0.041): Each additional year of age → 0.041-day increase in LOS
Severity (β₂ = 0.624): Each one-point increase → 0.624-day increase in LOS
Comorbidities (β₃ = 0.793): Each additional comorbidity → 0.793-day increase in LOS

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
section: Model Fit: R² vs. Adjusted R²
text:
Model Fit: R² vs. Adjusted R²
From the summary() output above:

R² = 0.648: 64.8% of variance in LOS is explained by the model
Adjusted R² = 0.645: Adjusted R² penalizes for the number of predictors and is preferred when comparing models with different numbers of variables



Why Adjusted R²?

Regular R² can only increase when you add more predictors, even if they have no real relationship.
Adjusted R² penalizes for the number of predictors. It only increases if a new predictor genuinely improves the model.

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Predicting LOS: By Hand
Let’s predict LOS for a new patient with Age = 75, Severity = 5, Comorbidities = 2:

Step 1: Recall the fitted equation
\[\widehat{\text{LOS}} = 1.31 + 0.041 \times \text{Age} + 0.624 \times \text{Severity} + 0.793 \times \text{Comorbidities}\]

Step 2: Plug in the values
\[\widehat{\text{LOS}} = 1.31 + 0.041 \times 75 + 0.624 \times 5 + 0.793 \times 2\]


Step 3: Calculate
\[\widehat{\text{LOS}} = 9.07 \text{ days}\]

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Predicting LOS: In R
R makes this easier with predict() — let’s predict for multiple patients at once:

Patient 1: Age 35, severity 2, no comorbidities
Patient 2: Age 75, severity 5, 2 comorbidities
Patient 3: Age 50, severity 8, 3 comorbidities
Patient 4: Age 80, severity 7, 5 comorbidities


example_patients <- data.frame(
  age = c(35, 75, 50, 80),
  severity_score = c(2, 5, 8, 7),
  num_comorbidities = c(0, 2, 3, 5)
)

example_patients$predicted_los <- predict(model_multiple, newdata = example_patients)
example_patients

A Puzzling Case
Can we predict hospital length of stay (LOS) from the number of comorbidities and medications a patient has?
Let’s check this. Load the dataset using the code below:

demo_data <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mba642-spring-26/mba642-spring-26.github.io/refs/heads/main/datasets/week11_multicollinearity.csv")

3 3                 2               6 3.3

Let’s Fit Three Models
Let’s fit three models and compare:

Comorbidities only
Medications only
Both Comorbidities and Medications


model_1 <- lm(los ~ num_comorbidities, data = demo_data)
model_2 <- lm(los ~ num_medications, data = demo_data)
model_3 <- lm(los ~ num_comorbidities + num_medications, data = demo_data)

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
What Happened?

Model 2 (medications alone): Significant positive effect (+0.28)
Model 3 (both together): Medications coefficient changes direction (-0.33)!
The same predictor tells a completely different story depending on what else is in the model



Why? The two predictors are highly correlated!

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
This Is Multicollinearity
Multicollinearity occurs when predictors are highly correlated with each other, making it difficult to separate their individual effects.

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
How to Diagnose: VIF
A commonly used metric is the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF):
\[\text{VIF}_j = \frac{1}{1 - R^2_j}\]
where \(R^2_j\) is the R² from regressing predictor \(j\) on all other predictors.
Rule of thumb: VIF > 10 indicates problematic multicollinearity.

We can get VIF using the vif() function from the car package:

library(car)

vif_values <- vif(model_3)
vif_values

num_comorbidities   num_medications 
         8.647367          8.647367

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
How to Handle Multicollinearity
When VIF is high, you have several options:

Keep the most theoretically important predictor and remove the redundant one
Combine them into a composite measure (e.g., “patient complexity index”)
Check the correlation matrix before modeling to catch it early

title: Linear Regression 1:  Simple and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Key Takeaways

Simple regression: How one factor relates to an outcome
Multiple regression: How several factors together relate to an outcome, each factor’s unique contribution holding others constant
OLS finds the line that minimizes the sum of squared residuals
R² tells you what percentage of variation your model explains; in multiple regression, use Adjusted R² which penalizes for adding unhelpful predictors
Interpreting coefficients: ask three questions: Direction? Magnitude? Significant?
Multicollinearity can completely mislead you about which predictors matter; check VIF

title: Linear Regression 2: Dummy Variables and Interaction Effects
text:
This lecture introduces two extensions to the linear regression framework from Week 11:

Dummy Variable Regression: Including categorical predictors in regression models

Binary categories (e.g., ERAS vs. Standard care)
Multi-level categories (e.g., Teaching vs. Community vs. Critical Access hospitals)

Interaction Effects: Testing whether the effect of one variable depends on another

Continuous × Categorical (e.g., does staffing effect vary by hospital ownership?)
Categorical × Categorical (e.g., does treatment effectiveness vary by insurance type?)
Continuous × Continuous (e.g., does PT session benefit depend on patient age?)

title: Linear Regression 2: Dummy Variables and Interaction Effects
section: Practice: Dummy Variables and Interaction Effects
text:
Practice: Dummy Variables and Interaction Effects






NoteYour Turn!



Practice fitting and interpreting regression models with dummy variables and interaction effects using a new healthcare scenario.



Scenario
You are a healthcare analyst evaluating hospital quality improvement initiatives across a national hospital network. Quality scores (0-100) measure overall hospital performance based on patient outcomes, safety, and patient experience.

Whether IT investment (e.g., electronic health records, clinical decision support systems) affects quality differently in teaching vs. non-teaching hospitals

This analysis will guide resource allocation and technology investment decisions across the hospital network.


Data Loading

title: Linear Regression 2: Dummy Variables and Interaction Effects
text:
Key Takeaways
Dummy Variables:

Allow categorical predictors in regression using 0/1 coding
For k categories, R creates k-1 dummy variables automatically
Coefficients represent differences from the reference category
Use factor(x, levels = c("Reference", ...)) to set the reference
Use emmeans() with pairs() for all pairwise comparisons

Interaction Effects:

An interaction means the effect of one variable depends on another
Use * in the formula to include both main effects and the interaction: lm(y ~ x1 * x2)
Three types: Continuous × Categorical, Categorical × Categorical, Continuous × Continuous
With interactions present, main effects represent the effect only for the reference group
To get the effect for other groups: add main effect + interaction coefficient

title: Linear Regression 2:  Dummy Variables and Interaction Effects
text:
Today’s Learning Goals
By the end of this lecture, you will be able to:

Create and interpret dummy variables for categorical predictors in regression (binary and multi-level)
Test and interpret interaction effects in regression
Compute marginal effects to describe how a predictor’s impact varies across groups

title: Linear Regression 2:  Dummy Variables and Interaction Effects
text:
Beyond Continuous Predictors
In Week 11, we used continuous predictors (e.g., wait time, staffing hours) to predict outcomes.


But many important variables in healthcare are categorical (e.g., hospital type, insurance status, treatment protocol, or region).


Moreover, the effect of a continuous variable can differ depending on those categories.



Dummy variables and interactions answer more nuanced questions:

Do outcomes differ across groups, after controlling for other factors?
Does the effect of one variable change depending on the level of another?

title: Linear Regression 2:  Dummy Variables and Interaction Effects
section: Why This Matters for Healthcare Management
text:
Why This Matters for Healthcare Management
These techniques directly support real management decisions:

Resource allocation: Should we prioritize staffing investments in non-profit hospitals, where the satisfaction payoff may be larger?
Cost management: Does the Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocol reduce length of stay equally across patient severity levels, or should we target it to specific groups?
Performance benchmarking: Are we comparing hospitals fairly if we don’t account for differences in patient mix and hospital type?

title: Linear Regression 2:  Dummy Variables and Interaction Effects
text:
Today’s Roadmap

Dummy Variables – Including categorical predictors (binary and multi-level) in regression
Interaction Effects – Testing whether the effect of one variable depends on another

Continuous x Categorical
Categorical x Categorical
Continuous x Continuous

title: Linear Regression 2:  Dummy Variables and Interaction Effects
text:
What Are Dummy Variables?
Dummy variables (indicator variables) are binary variables representing categorical group membership using 0s and 1s.


For a categorical variable with k categories, we create k-1 dummy variables, with one category serving as the reference group.


Example: 3 Hospital Types (Teaching, Community, Critical Access) → 2 dummy variables:

Dummy 1: Teaching (1 if Teaching, 0 otherwise)
Dummy 2: Critical Access (1 if Critical Access, 0 otherwise)
Community = reference (both dummies = 0)

title: Linear Regression 2:  Dummy Variables and Interaction Effects
text:
When to Use Dummy Variables
Regression requires numerical inputs, but categorical variables are not inherently numerical. Simply assigning numbers (e.g., Teaching=1, Community=2, Critical Access=3) would imply a false ordering.

Dummy variables solve this by representing group membership as 0s and 1s, allowing us to:

Include categorical predictors in regression (hospital type, insurance status, treatment group)
Test whether group differences are statistically significant while controlling for other variables
Quantify the magnitude of differences between categories

title: Linear Regression 2:  Dummy Variables and Interaction Effects
text:
Example Case: Treatment Protocol Comparison
The problem: Traditional surgical recovery involves extended hospital stays, which are costly and can lead to complications.


A better approach: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocols use evidence-based practices: better pain management, early mobilization, and earlier nutrition.



Let’s compare patient outcomes between Standard care and ERAS protocols to quantify the treatment effect using a dummy variable.

title: Linear Regression 2:  Dummy Variables and Interaction Effects
text:
Loading Packages and Data
Let’s load the required packages and the data using the code below:

library(tidyverse)    # data wrangling and visualization
library(emmeans)      # pairwise comparisons across groups
library(interactions) # visualizing interaction effects

surgical_data <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mba642-spring-26/mba642-spring-26.github.io/refs/heads/main/datasets/week12_surgical_data.csv")
head(surgical_data, 5)

  X patient_id protocol age  bmi surgery_complexity length_of_stay
1 1          1 Standard  77 27.3                  3            9.8
2 2          2 Standard  56 27.1                  3           10.4
3 3          3 Standard  59 23.7                  3            9.3
4 4          4     ERAS  49 32.8                  3            9.6
5 5          5 Standard  74 23.8                  3           11.0

title: Linear Regression 2:  Dummy Variables and Interaction Effects
text:
Setting the Reference Category
We use factor() to set “Standard” as the reference category:

surgical_data <- surgical_data %>%
  mutate(protocol = factor(protocol, levels = c("Standard", "ERAS")))




When we include protocol in the model, R automatically creates the dummy variable for us.
The first level specified in factor() (here, "Standard") becomes the reference category.

  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, width = 0.4) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.3, size = 1) +
  labs(
    x = "Treatment Protocol",
    y = "Length of Stay (days)",
    title = "Does ERAS Protocol Affect Length of Stay?"
  ) +

  theme(legend.position = "none")

Fitting the Model

Now we can fit a linear regression model to estimate the effect of the ERAS protocol on length of stay, controlling for age, BMI, and surgery complexity
We can use the same lm() function as before, just including the protocol variable as a predictor


model_protocol <- lm(length_of_stay ~ protocol + age + bmi + surgery_complexity,
                     data = surgical_data)
summary(model_protocol)

title: Linear Regression 2:  Dummy Variables and Interaction Effects
text:
Manual Calculation with Dummy Variables
Patient profile: A 65-year-old patient with BMI of 30 and surgery complexity of 2.

The fitted equation:
\[\widehat{\text{LOS}} = 3.218 + -1.788(\text{ERAS}) + 0.027(\text{Age}) + 0.048(\text{BMI}) + 1.497(\text{Complexity})\]


Standard protocol (ERAS = 0):
\[\widehat{\text{LOS}} = 3.218 + -1.788(0) + 0.027(65) + 0.048(30) + 1.497(2) = 9.41 \text{ days}\]


ERAS protocol (ERAS = 1):
\[\widehat{\text{LOS}} = 3.218 + -1.788(1) + 0.027(65) + 0.048(30) + 1.497(2) = 7.62 \text{ days}\]

title: Linear Regression 2:  Dummy Variables and Interaction Effects
section: The Difference Is Exactly the Coefficient
text:
The Difference Is Exactly the Coefficient
For the same patient (age 65, BMI 30, complexity 2):

Standard protocol: 9.41 days
ERAS protocol: 7.62 days
Difference: -1.79 days = ERAS coefficient (-1.79)


 The dummy variable coefficient represents the difference in predicted outcomes between the two groups, holding all other variables constant. This is true regardless of the patient profile we plug in.

title: Linear Regression 2:  Dummy Variables and Interaction Effects
text:
Why k-1 Dummy Variables?
When a categorical variable has more than two levels, we need k-1 dummy variables (where k is the number of categories).


Including a dummy for every category would create perfect multicollinearity.

The dummy variables would sum to 1 for every observation, perfectly correlated with the intercept.



 Each of the k-1 dummy coefficients represents the difference between that category and the reference category.

title: Linear Regression 2:  Dummy Variables and Interaction Effects
text:
What Is an Interaction Effect?
An interaction effect occurs when the effect of one variable on the outcome depends on the value of another variable.


Mathematically:
\[Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \beta_3 (X_1 \times X_2) + \epsilon\]


The interaction coefficient \(\beta_3\) captures how the effect of \(X_1\) changes across levels of \(X_2\) (or vice versa)

title: Linear Regression 2:  Dummy Variables and Interaction Effects
text:
When to Use Interactions
Use interaction terms when:

Theory or prior research suggests an effect should vary across groups
Visual inspection shows different slopes for different groups
You want to test whether an intervention works differently for different populations or conditions



Examples:

A medication may work better for younger vs. older patients
Additional staffing may have different impacts in big vs. small hospitals
A new policy may affect urban and rural hospitals differently

section: Computing Marginal Effects at Different Ages
text:
Computing Marginal Effects at Different Ages

Age 30: Effect = 0.82 + (30 × -0.02) = 0.22 points per session
Age 50: Effect = 0.82 + (50 × -0.02) = -0.18 points per session
Age 70: Effect = 0.82 + (70 × -0.02) = -0.58 points per session



The effect of PT sessions changes dramatically with age. Positive for younger patients, potentially negative for older patients.

Interpreting the Visualization
Simple Slopes Analysis:

Age 30: Positive slope – PT sessions are beneficial
Age 50: Negative slope – PT sessions are associated with worse outcomes
Age 70: Negative slope – PT sessions are associated with worse outcomes


 Key insight:

The interaction creates a crossover effect where the treatment benefit reverses direction in different subgroups.
In practice, this would warrant investigation into confounding factors (e.g., sicker older patients may be prescribed more PT sessions, making PT appear less effective).

title: Linear Regression 2:  Dummy Variables and Interaction Effects
text:
Key Takeaways

Dummy variables let us include categorical predictors in regression using 0s and 1s
We can not only compare two categories or groups, but also multiple categories by creating k-1 dummy variables
Use emmeans() for pairwise comparisons across multi-level categorical variables
Interaction effects test whether the effect of one variable depends on another
In interaction models, main effects have conditional interpretations (at zero or reference level)
Use probe_interaction() for visualizing interaction effects

title: Logistic Regression: Predicting Binary Outcomes in Healthcare
text:
1.1 What is it?
Simple logistic regression models the relationship between one predictor variable (continuous or categorical) and a binary outcome (0 or 1). It estimates the probability of the outcome occurring as a function of the predictor, using the logistic (S-shaped) curve to keep predictions between 0 and 1.

title: Logistic Regression: Predicting Binary Outcomes in Healthcare
text:
1.2 When to Use It
Use simple logistic regression when:

Your outcome variable is binary (two possible values: 0/1, yes/no)
You have one predictor variable you want to examine
You want to understand how the predictor affects the probability of the outcome
You want to quantify the effect using log odds ratios and odds ratios

title: Logistic Regression: Predicting Binary Outcomes in Healthcare
text:
1.3 Example Case: Predicting Hospital Readmission
You are a quality improvement analyst at a regional hospital. Hospital readmissions within 30 days are a major concern because they indicate potential gaps in care quality and result in financial penalties under Medicare’s Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program.
Your hospital has been assessing patient discharge readiness (measured on a 1-10 scale at discharge) and wants to understand: Does discharge readiness predict the likelihood of 30-day readmission?
The hypothesis is that patients who feel more ready for discharge have a better understanding of their follow-up care instructions, are more confident in managing their health at home, and therefore are less likely to be readmitted.
The Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program (HRRP), established by the Affordable Care Act, penalizes hospitals with excess readmissions for specific conditions. Research has shown that perceived readiness for hospital discharge is associated with post-discharge outcomes including readmission rates, though the relationship is influenced by multiple factors including patient demographics, clinical complexity, and post-discharge support systems.

title: Logistic Regression: Predicting Binary Outcomes in Healthcare
text:

Variables in the dataset:

patient_id: Unique identifier for each patient (1 to 200)
discharge_readiness: Discharge readiness score (1-10 scale, where higher scores indicate greater readiness for discharge)
age: Patient age in years
comorbidities: Number of chronic health conditions (e.g., diabetes, hypertension, heart disease)

Let’s visually look at the relationship between discharge readiness and readmission:

p1

title: Logistic Regression: Predicting Binary Outcomes in Healthcare
text:
2.1 What is it?
Multiple logistic regression extends simple logistic regression by including two or more predictor variables to predict a binary outcome. The model estimates the independent effect of each predictor while holding all other predictors constant, just like multiple linear regression, but for binary outcomes.

title: Logistic Regression: Predicting Binary Outcomes in Healthcare
text:
2.2 When to Use It
Use multiple logistic regression when:

Your outcome variable is binary (0/1)
You have two or more predictor variables (continuous, categorical, or both)
You want to control for confounding variables
You want to understand the independent effect of each predictor

Multiple logistic regression enables us to:

Control for confounding variables (factors that might distort the relationship we’re studying)
Make more accurate predictions by incorporating more information

title: Logistic Regression: Predicting Binary Outcomes in Healthcare
section: 2.3 Example Case: Comprehensive Readmission Risk Model
text:
2.3 Example Case: Comprehensive Readmission Risk Model
In the simple regression section, we used only discharge readiness to predict readmission. But what if that effect was partly due to confounding? For example, younger, healthier patients may feel more ready for discharge AND are naturally less likely to be readmitted. Without controlling for age and comorbidities, we might be overstating the true effect of discharge readiness.
Our readmit_data dataset (n = 200) already includes additional variables we can use to build a more comprehensive model:

discharge_readiness: Discharge readiness score (1-10 scale)
age: Patient age in years
comorbidities: Number of chronic health conditions (e.g., diabetes, hypertension, heart disease)
insurance: Insurance type (Private, Medicare, or Medicaid) — a categorical predictor
readmitted: Whether the patient was readmitted within 30 days (1 = yes, 0 = no)

title: Logistic Regression: Predicting Binary Outcomes in Healthcare
text:
Key Takeaways

When to Use Logistic Regression

Use logistic regression when your outcome variable is binary (two possible values)
Use glm(outcome ~ predictors, data = data, family = binomial) in R
The model predicts the probability of the event occurring



Interpreting Coefficients
Ask three questions for each coefficient:

Direction: Is the log odds ratio positive or negative? (Positive = increases odds; Negative = decreases odds)
Magnitude: What is the odds ratio? How much do the odds change per unit increase in the predictor?
Significance: Is p < 0.05? (But practical significance matters too!)



Log Odds Ratios vs. Odds Ratios



Measure
No Effect
Decreases Risk
Increases Risk




Log Odds Ratio
= 0
< 0
> 0


Odds Ratio
= 1
< 1
> 1





Converting Between Measures
Probability → Odds → Log Odds
\[\text{Odds} = \frac{p}{1-p}\]
\[\text{Log Odds} = \ln(\text{Odds})\]
Log Odds → Odds → Probability
\[\text{Odds} = e^{\text{Log Odds}}\]
\[\text{Probability} = \frac{\text{Odds}}{1 + \text{Odds}}\]


Simple vs. Multiple Logistic Regression








Aspect
Simple
Multiple




Predictors
One
Two or more


Interpretation
Direct effect
Effect controlling for other variables


Use case
Initial exploration
Comprehensive modeling


Confounding
Not addressed
Can be controlled





Model Evaluation

Accuracy measures overall correct predictions but can be misleading with imbalanced outcomes
Use the confusion matrix (classification table) to see where the model makes errors (false positives vs. false negatives)
In healthcare, consider which type of error is more costly for your specific application
